LANDLORDS AND FARMERS.

Wno can tell at the present moment what
the contest now going on in the agricultural
districts will end in?

There does not appear to be the least chance
that the fight will be fought out with'reason
or moderation. On one side there is ignorance,
poverty, distrust. On the other, selfishness, a
stolid sense of mastership, and a belief in the
degradation of lab Our as a providential condi-
tion of life. Were the condition of mind on
both sides, or even on one side, higher, such a
contest might lead to mutual concessions
and wiser understandings as to the special
claims belonging to both sides, and to a settle:.
Mont from which the farmer, as well as the
'labourer, might derive lasting advantage. Nor
does theie appear to be any hope of interven-
tion by intelligent third parties who might act
as arbitrators, and bring about some compro-
mise fair and equitable alike to master and
man.

The claim of the men is not unreasonable.
Sixteen shillings a week is not too much; it is
too little. It looks large as compared with
twelve shillings, but this is because the
smaller sum is shamefully and scandalously
inadequate for the support of a family. It is
a real disgrace to our national character that
years ago, pay generations since, that some-
thing approaching to justice was not done to
the agricultural labourers of England. Not to-
daj, not. yesterday, nor last year, but two
hundred years ago or even more, this question
ought to have been raised. The wealth of the
landowners of England and the substantial
comfort of the farmers of England arc un-
natural and anomalous side by side with the
poverty and, privations of the labourers. And
the insulting nonsense now talked by land-
lords and gentletnen farmers is simply dis-
graceful, sickening, abominable.
Nothing, however, could be truer than to
say there is no practical use in blaming the
present generation for the sins of the past;
for Could anything be more unjust than to
revenge the evil doings of past generations on
the men of the present. But when "parsons and
squires?' meet togetlier now in their chambers
of agriculture and elsewhere, to abuse the
labourers and. rail against agitators, and
against anything and everything that tends to
disquiet the starving workers, it would be a
neglect of a serious and important public duty
not to tell thorn how un-Christian, how anti-
Christian, how absolutely inhuman and fool-
ish their language is, and how infinitely
worse than the worst agitators they are in
precipitating a blind social conflict, in
setting, in the worst way, "class, against
class," in provoking a war .between labour
and capital, between hunger and property,
which will be a war ".to the knife," if the
labourers aro to wage it in a spirit corre-

sponding to that at present displayed by land-
lords and farmers.

At a meeting held some, days since by the
Chamber of Agriculture at Banbury, Mr.
WESTOVER read a paper on the dispute at
present going on in the agricultural districts;
and if this gentleman in any way represents
the ideas and feelings of landowners and
farmers, it may truly be said that, so far as.
they are concerned, no peace can be made or
ought to be made, until the doctrines they
hold are utterly subverted and cast out by the
action of the labourers, backed by the hearty
approval and liberal support of every man
who, even in the faintest way, believes in the
dignity of human life and the progress of
human society.
This manurges the introduction and appli-
cation of steam power to farming, that the
human agent may be loss a necessity to the
farmer; and this ought not to be objected to,
ad no sensible person wishes men to perform
drudgery to which 9team and iron and wood
may be applied. That men should benefit by
their own ingenuity, that the machine should
be brought in aid of the man, is right and
natural. Every humane person wishes for
this—not that men may be superseded and
starved, but that they may have leisure, rest,
abundance, and comfort. A clergyman, the
Rev. C. W. HOLBEOII) presided, whilst this
man read his paper, and we are not
informed that he administered any rebuke
while sentence after Beaten() of this devil's
doctrine was doled out. These words are
used advisedly and are far too weak to charac-
terise the meaning of the reader. He declared
that the Revised Code placed the standard of
education too high for the village school. The
teaching, he said, " would drive them
from agricultural pursuits," which to him
seemed quite an unpardonable thing,
that is, he would not drive them from
their ill-paid working and starving brutal
condition by instruction, by knowledge, by
what would give them higher desires and
larger capabilities. He would keep them in
their old blissful ignorance, their long-eon-
tinned bestial stupidity akin in intellect to
the horses and hogs amongst which they pass
their lives. And when they gave up the more
degraded and worst paid occupation fer some-
thing else, he was anxious that it should not.
for anything higher or bettor. Nothing of
this sort seemed to enter his head. What he
desires he has stated with the utmost plain-
ness, that they should be supers() ded ancl driven
out by machinery, and it may be presumed
starved into the acceptance of low wages, and
in the end driven to ;finish their lives in the
workhouse and

Weekly catch,
The morsel tossed by law-forced charity,
And died so slowly, that none;could call it murder."
. But one of the most curious things in this
man's paper was his attempt to condemn
education for the wretched old threadbare
reason which has been used by every dishonest
bigot in every part of the world ever since the
name of GOD has been made a cover to hide
the knaveries of men. ",I a misnomer,"
says Mr. IVE6TOVER, "to call that education,
Which ignored the teaching of the duty to
,the,
ciftEATOR and to each other," What 'will Mr.
FORSTEIt say to this grateful return made for
sacrifice of
,Principle to suit the squires? or
what can any person think of a person who has
the audacity to give his hearers to understand

that our national teaching ignores duty to GOD
and to our neighbours.

What these men mean is that the teaching
of the country does not put the squire in the
place of the Ararroirrv, and does not teach the
children of the poor the duty of crawling in
the dust before their "pastors and masters."
The resolutions of this meeting were not
quite as strong as the language of Mr.
WESTOVER. The meeeting took out of the
first resolution its condemnation of education,
but there cannot be any doubt that the gentle-
men who did so hate learning worse than
"asp or toad," that they are frightened into
panic by the anticipated spread of knowledge
amongst their workers. And well they may.
Who can doubt that even the most limited
instruction will put such promptings of man-
hod into the poorest peasant's heart, will
inevitably lift him above that sickening ser-
vility of soul by which he is at present
marked as with a brand. Our, greatest
Englishman declared that—
'lgnorance is the curse of God,
Knowledge the wing wherewith we fly to heaven."
But Mr. W.}:sTovEß and his friends think other-
wise. They know that they can only carry
on the grinding oppression they exercise by
preserving ignorance; boned they cry out
against education, just as they would against
anything which would strengthen the hands
of their labourers, knowing, as they do, that
the first use they would make of any new
power they might attain would be to compel
the granting of more equitable terms of ser-
vice.

As a matter of course the Banbury Chamber
condemned very strongly, in one of their re-
solutions, the excessive demands of the men)
"as tending to destroy all confidence between
master and man, and to set class against
class." It Would have been well if these poi-
sons had told us *hat the confidenoe between
them and their man amounts to; or if they
gad explained whether their present condition
is not one of "class against class." These
high-hounding phrases are of no value. There
is no *confidence, there can be no confidence,
where' suoh a .system as that in which these
people live exists. Fire and water might as
well be expected to unite in harmony as
plethora and poverty. "Fine words butter
no parsnips." The proverb is musty i but true.
The employers may say what they like as to
confidence between them and their men, but
thorough earnest speech of the labourers giVes
a far better idea as to the actual state of
things. They are beginning to "unpack their
hearts," and when they have got a little more
used to the sound of their own voices, they
will no doubt give the world pretty fully to
understand how scant the love is by which
they and their masters are bound together.
The WESTOVERS, and the crowds like them in
the agricultural districts, who are standing
face to facie with what may be the beginning'
of a gigantic social revolution, if not now at
no very distant time, babble like half-angry)"
half-crazy men,. not seeming to comprehend in
the least the moaning of them long deferred
demands. They seem utterly incapable .of
asking themselves a single sensible question
as to whether, in such a country as England,
starvation and suffering eiln exist side by side
with an overflowing opulence, and a luxury
which, by its contrast with squalor, is shame-
ful in the eyes of GOD and man. It is folly to
say the farmorsican't afford it. They must

LLOYD SONES.

STRIKE OF AGRICULTURAL
LABOURERS.

Fr was announced in a . "leader" of the
Daily Telegraph of March 13th, 1872, that
the agricultural labourers of South
,Warwick-
shire were meditating a strike, "which it was
very glad to, hear "that they should have
done so gonoratiOns ago ;"
.but it Was "bettor
late than. never ;" and gave the movement
every encouragement'. In the same paper,
March" 21st, another leader said, we learn
that at a great meeting held near Mollinghan,
Oxford, the men demand 18s per week and
shorter hours of labour. It iris ultimate&
agreed that they tdiould form a coalition with
the labour union of Warwickshire. The
Willisbourno fain hands- are still out on
strike,
,and two. hundred' pounds were distribu-
ted among them last week. Funds for the
further support if men are, it is aided,
flowing in rapidly, and the trades unionists in
the towns are 'coining forward to support the
peasants in the struggle. "These brief wards,"
it continues, " are pregnant with the gravest
meaning; and in the interest'of all Classes it
believes the representatives of public opinion
dispassionately, to point out, how far such a
movement as this., which bids fair to spread
wider over the country, is justifiable, and
what are the prospects of ultimate success."
I entirely agree with every word of the
foregoing Whether immediate success follows
this movement or net it is net less important,
not merely to the labourers' themselves, but to
the country at large. The Rev. CAlsio'
GIUDLESTONE has, in his exertions for years
past in behalf or the agricultural 'labourers,
made known their :condition to the public as
being the most oppressed and degraded by the
lowest of low wages of all 'daises who live
by wages, Or, as in their ease, it may be said
barely exist by them. '

It may be very true, as laid down by Mr.
J. S. Max, that the low wages of• these
labourers were caused by their undue increase
of population, and that no permanent rise in.
wages can take place, Unless population, by
moral restraint, is kept down to the number
that will ensure the wages they demand.
But this was the ease in France before its first
revolution, wired the peasantry sulfured uu-
heard of privations. By the law of demand and
supply they were doomed to hopeless misery,
but that did not justify the landlords and the
e
rich farmers in grinding them to powder, or
those who told them "to at grass" if they
were hungry. There Was over population, it
is true, among the labourers, but it wai
because the 'classes above them had more than
their share of the efuties produce,
and
not
because there was too little for all. And bit-
terly did these landlords and rich farmers suffer
for this state of things, which doubtless they
had no hand in bringing about, but which they

had not the sense or the humanity to alter or
to ameliorate. In like manner, though
probably with not the: Same rest-fit,
.are our
"local landowners." The same newspaper,
March 22nd, tells us, "And farmers, assisted
by not a few clergymen, are denouncing the
movement, and are warning their dependents
from joining it. At a public meeting, presided
over by Sir CILIRLES MORDAIINT, resolutions
wore p lased deprecating any combination among
the labourers as tending to foster discord between
there and their employers; affirming that, in
the interest of the labourers themselves, every
effort should be made to dissuade them from
joining
,unions, and recommending them to
withdraw if they had joined, and declaring,
with respect to the Willesbourne strike, that
the demands were excessive, but at the same
time declining to indicate what would be
reasonable." Those resolutions were printed
*Mt Sir CHAILLES MORDAUNT'S signature to
them, and posted up in the surrounding
villages.
The Banbury Chamber of Commerce has
called a special meeting for Tuesday, March
26th, to discuss the
,questions involved by
the strike. The resolutions to be submitted
agree with those adopted by the local land-
holders in pronouncing the demands excessive
and deprecating agitation in the villages.
Their severity is, however, redeemed by a re-
commendation that a labourers' conference
should be organised by the Chamber of Agri-
culture. In view of the reiterated desire of
the men for arbitration, such proposal has a good
chance of finding acceptance among them.
New, hero is the old story-188. a week
is an excessive demand. Wages ranging
between Bs, and 12s. a week are, without
doubt, what it is desired they should be
-contented with, although the local land-
()inners , and farmers have not the hardi-
hood to indicate what they would deem
reasonable. Instead, of' deprecating this
movement and trying to put it down, the
landowners and farmers ought to rejoice that
it has taken place, for it is of all others a
circumstance which if successful, will give
stability' to their position and render impoi-
bible to them a similar fate to that of the
French nobility and farmers who were swept
from the face of the earth for the sumo kind of
oppression. To avert such a catastrophe,
Success must attend the movement of the
agricultural labourers ; and trades unionists
will do well to give them every assistance.

I find by the Daily Telegraph of March
28, that the Rev. Canon GIRDLESTONiI has
'written io the 'Warwickshire labourers on
strike, " enjoining them to remember how much
better off they wore than tho hinds of North
Devon, who had to live on Bs. a week, and pay
high rents, without any perquisites save two
quarts of bad eider. He had understood that the
Warwickshire employers wore willing to give
15s. a week, that they provided good cottages at
moderate rents, and that there was a prospect
of a partial holiday being granted on Saturday
by stopping work at four o'clock."

"Blessed are the peacemakers," and the
Rev. CANON is not to be blamed for trying to
reconcile the qoarrel between the labourers
and their employers at additional wages. But
the Rev. CANON knows well, none better, that
the reason of this dispute is that there is at
present a comparative dearth of labourers in
Warwickshire, and that acting upon the doc-
trine so often preached to them on the laws of
demand and supply, they have taken advan-
tage of the fact that the demand for their
labour is much blow its supply, and require
18s. per week, on precisely the same grounds
that the labourers of North Devon, by their
over supply of labourers, were made to accept
" Bs. a Week and two quarts of bad eider."

I am informed that the Rev. CANON has
lately received Church preferment, which he
deserves from his strenuous exertions in behalf
of the agricultural labourers. I wish I was
sure it was for that he obtained it. Is there
not a stroke of .irony, in referring them, for
their s.•lions consideration, to the hinds of
North Devon,- with their Bs. a wok, high
rents, and two (itt tits of bad eider P—knowing
as he does, that according to the law of demand
and supply, their employers, the supply of
hbourer6 being the same, tvoul4 euly be tec,

happy to reduce them to the same condition as
the unhappy "hinds of North Devon."
This over-population of which we have
spoken is artificial, and is in consequence of
the land being, by the laws of primogeniture
and entail, in the hands of a few landed
proprietors. In France and elsewhere where
the land is cultivated by peasant proprietors,
there is no over-population; and, muse.
quently, no grinding oppression like that
endured by the "hinds of North Devon," or
that from which the labourers of Warwick-
shire are trying to emerge.
Among the many modes of assistance these
labourers are receiving, there is none more
likely to have permanent effect than the trying
to induce them to emigrate by sending—as I
find, by the Daily Telegraph of April 2nd, has
been done—Mr. THOS. CONNOLLY, as an emi-
gration agent and lecturer, among them. Once
get them to emigrate, and a peimanent rise in
the wages of the agricultural labourers
throughout the whole length and breadth of
the land is ensured in just the proportion they
can be got to adopt this remedy. They are
exactly the sort of immigrants the Canadian
fanners want.

articles.title: T. J. DUNNING.
articles.text:
T. J. DUNNING.

THE CAUSES OF EVIL AND OF GOOD.

I am very glad that my much esteemed
friend Mr. BARTON has stated his objections to
the views respeating the causes of evil and of
good, which I have been endeavouring to
make plain in the BEE-HIVE. lam glad
that he has done so, because in meeting ob-
jections directly a favourable opportunity is
given for clearing up points which may have
been insUffiaiently explained. That he is not
satisfied with my explanations may proceed
from one or both of two causes. Either that
my explanations have not yet been made '
sufficiently clear, or that he has not read and
considered them with sufficient attention and
care. However much may be due to the
former cause, it is evident, from several of his
remarks, that not rt. little is owing to the
latter. For views are attributed to me which
I have most plainly disavowed. When I
look at his objections I cannot but feel sur-
prised and sorry that he has not thought it
worth his While to consider more carefully a
subject of such overwhelming importance.
And surely to consider well, to examine care-
fully the facts of a subject before judging it,
is the very first rule to be observed in the
pursuit of knowledge; and is the first duty,
to others and to himself, of oue who assumes
the aloe of a critics. He says " I cannot
believe that the necoesarian doctrine is news.
Emily calculated to produce charity, or that
the belief in it is essential for individual or
social reform." Nor do I believe it. First,
because the mere neoessarian has very often
no more charity than the libertarian. And;
again, because in this doctrine the denial of
the highly important truth that man has a
power of self-government, is confounded with
the assertion of the truth that man is the
creature of causation. But the knowledge of
this truth (relative to causation), with the
knowledge of the eauses.of evil and of good to
man, is "calculated to produce charity," and is
" essential, for individual and social reform."
How it is so I have pointed out very plainly,
I think, to any one who will read carefully
my description of the fiiets of the subject.
(BEE-lI[VE, March 16.) Bat he thinks
I have "out the ground from my feet by ad-
mitting that man has a power of self-govern-
ment.' On the contrary, it must be self-
evident upon a little consideration, that I have
got my feet set firmly on the rock of truth by
doing so, instead, of having them in the
quagmire of error into which the neeessarians
have plunged themselves by confounding the
denial of man's power of self-government with
the assertion of the truth relative to causation.
I have removed a powerful cause of evil (the
ignorance and denial of man's power of self-
government), and have put in its place a power-
ful cause of good—the knowledge of this power
—not the more common instinctive knowledge
of it, but the understimding of it.

In his next remarks my good friend says—
"Whoa a man unjustly blames or punishes
another, it is not because he is ignorant of the
doctrine of the necessary origin of tilts feelings

and conduct, but simply because, from de_
fectiVe organization, or imperfect or bad edu-
cation, his selfish or egotistic propensities pre-
vail over his sympathetic or altruistic (regard
7or others) feelings." I will simply correct
this statement by saying that " When a man
tnjustly blatnes or punishes another, it is be-
ittuse" he has Wen caused to acquire erro-
neous ideas relative to the causes of evil and
of good to man, and because, in consequence
of the influence of these erroneous ideas (as
causes of evil) upon his moral nature, and of
the other injurious influences of the present
state of society, consequent upon these erro-
neous ideas, ignorantly irascible and unkind
habits of fooling have been strongly developed
within him.

Mr. BARTON then says that "We can,
and de, modify man's feelings and con-
duct"—as I say. But I say, further, that
when we have acquired the knowledge of the
causes of evil and of good—true enlightenment
—and enlightened goodness, and not before,
we shall ho able to modify them by education,
so as to make them right. And that, hitherto,
men have never been able so to modify them,
because they have never yet had this know-
ledge and goodness.
He then says that " praise and blame are
affleient motives—the one to encourage good
conduct, the other to check misconduct."
That they are very inefficient as means of
education is proved by the fact that they have
never produced a character of trite enlighten-
ment and enlightened goodness. They are
very inefficient as means to modify man's feel-
ings and conduct beneficially, for the pimple
reason (simple when it is known) that they do
not remove the causes of had feelings and con-
duct. And so long as they are not employed
under the guidance of the knowledge of the
causes of evil and of good to man, they are
themselves to a considerable extent causes of
bad feelings and conduct. They are educa-
tional and social makeshifts, which men are
obliged to use while they are ignorant of the
causes of evil and of good, and while, there-
fore, they are unable to substitute causes of
good for causes of evil.

He then says, " Man does not generally act
from knowledge or intellect, but front feeling."
fie evidently does not SO3, or Sees very
vaguely, how much our habits of feeling are
dependent upon our habits of thought. And
he does not see at all the effects of habits of
erroneous thought in reforonce to the causes
of evil and of good, to influonoo Man inju-
riously in his Social feelings. Nor does be see,
of coarse, the efroots which. will be produeed
by habits
,of correct thought in
.reference to
the causes of evil and of good to man, to in-
fluence him beneficially. Why has he Written
all these objections? Not merely because he
has certain feelings upon the subject, but
because the feelings which he has are conse-
quent upon certain thoughts, which he would
not have if he had acquired the knowledge of
causes. He next says, "It is mit any know-
ledge—any intellectual power—that will re-
generate society, but LOVE, under the
guidance of intellect, to secure a right direc-
tion and a fruitful end." I, too, say that
what is wanted is love, under the guidance of
intellect. But before love can be under the
guidance of intellect, "to secure a right direc-
tion and a fruitful end," intellect must be
under the guidance of the knowledge of
causes. We have seen in the past what love,
under the guidance of intellect, has been able
to effect, while intellect has been unen-
lightened by this knowledge. There will be
plenty of love in the world, and plenty of in-
tellect to guide it, when intellect is under this
guidance. Intellect without this knowledge
is a blind guide, as is evident front the expe-
rience of the past.
He then says, "I believe a great cause of
evil . . . to be selfishness." True. But
selfishness is a secondary cause of evil. It is
one of the evil effects of the fundamental
cause of evil; that is, of an education under
the influence of ignorance and erroneous
ideas relative to the causes of evil and of
good to man. I: do not think this need be
pointed out more plainly than I described it
in the BEE-HIVE of March 16. And can
anything be more obvious than that "the
best way to destroy or modify this evil (sei_

APRIL 6, 1872.

tishness), and to develop° the counter-
acting virtue -- love or sympathy,"
is to remove the causes of the evil
feeling, and to substitute for them the
causes of the good feeling? Of course with
young children "every available means must
be used to exercise the benevolent instincts."
But the means for this purpose which are
available to the educator who is ignorant of
the causes of evil and of good, are extremely
limited, in comparison with those which will he
, available to the educator who has acquired
this knowledge, and the enlightened goodness
which can never exist without it. In proof of
this, see what Mr. OWEN effected at New
Lanark; and see the wretched moral results
of ordinary education in all classes in the
present system. All "noble and generous
ideas and examples," and all " social activity
for the common good," which can exist while
men are ignorant and in error in reference to
the causes of evil and of good, must be ex-
tremely defective. They cannot be more than
the ideas, and examples, and activities of men
who are very defective, intellectually, and
morally.
With respect to the "positive religion
of humanity," it will have to be very
much improved, under the guidance of the
knowledge of the causes of evil and of
good, before it can be effectual to produce
"peace on earth and good will
among
men." As it is at present, it is little, if
anything, more than a new combination of old .
expedients, somewhat modified, which have
been proved inefficient to regenerate society
by centuries of most calamitous failure.
Nothing can bo more than this which does not
emanate from, and include, the knowledge of
the causes of evil and of good to man. The
primary cause of the evil effects which my
good friend attributes to " theological reli-
gion," is in reality the erroneous ideas in
reference to causes which are the basis of the
present social system. When this cause is
removed, its effects will cease to be produced.
I am well aware that with all the explana-
tions which can be given, and with all the
references to facts which can be made, there
will he very many who, having passed their
lives in ignorance of causes and effects in
reference to man, and having therefore been
caused to acquire firmly-rooted habits of
erroneous thought and, injurious feeling, will
not be able to understand this great subject
until they can see it practically exemplified.
But there will be many who will be able to
understand and appreciate it, when it can be
brought under their notice with sufficient
plainness. And these will be quite sufficient
to produce the practical example which alone

IIENRY TRAVIS.

THE AGRICULTURAL LABOURER.

A writer in the Times of Monday, says " It
is not so long since that a medical officer at-
tached to the Privy Council Office made $
Report in which he described the plyßie,al
power qf the country labourer as in a pr-ogress
of rapid deterioration through an insufficiency
of food fit to sustain his strength."
Now this is a most mdmentous announce-
ment, and that there is some truth illit
evidenced by the fact that trades unions are
being attempted in rural districts amongst this
class for the purpose of enforcing their rights
to higher wages and shorter hours of labour.
Is it not natural that this class should feel
that their only mode of bettering their cell-
dition was the enhancement of the illensl
price of labour? but what are we to say to
those (would-be) champions of the labouring
classes, especially those who are able to writs
to their names, when we find such a dis-
play of ignorance on "cause and drat "
amongst them as we find in the ranks of the
labourers themselves for instance? There los.
not been a word said yet, or at least we have not
seen or heard one, on tho question of bettering
the condition of the labouring classes by takie_g
away those oppressive fiscal burdens which
, bar the way and obstruct the process that
leads to bettering the condition of all classes
by enhancing the purchase power of their
wages or other income, especially of those
With only mnderate means. The time has

arrived when a tax upon tea, coffee, sugar,
and especially malt, is as much a. tax on the
people's bread as the direct tax on corn used
to be, as we remember in times gone by.
just consider for a moment the following
facts :

1. The "rural labourer in a state of rapid
deterioration through insufficiency of food."
2. That the yeoman class (or farmers' sons)
and artisans are leaving our shores in order
to settle down in a country that by dint of
circumstances, and in the nature of things
(brought about by hostile tariffs) must inevitably
become our worst enemies, at the rate of about
200,000 per annum.

(This in itself is enough to corroborate the
Medical officer's Report alluded to above.)
3. Again, the artiele in the Times says—
" The English farmer, as a producer or beef
and corn is subject to the severest competition.
Cattle are brought to us from all parts of
Europe, and every week a fleet of ships
arrives from the Southern hemisphere with
preserved meats for English use. The price of
corn and: the limit of profitable cultivation
among us are prescribed by the harvests of the
Continent and America."
4. In fame of all this, the present
CHANCELLOR of the EXCHEQUER is determined
to perpetuate that policy which tends to
enhance the price of those necessaries and
comforts of life whioh constitute the farmers'
and their labourers' breakfast, dinner and
supper table.

• 6. If these commodities are not to be freed
from taxation it follows that labour and capital
are still to be unduly weighted in their race of
competition with the foreign produoer, no
matter whether agriculture or manufacture.
6. If the Malt tax were repealed, the farmers
of Ireland would. be able to share with the
foreigner that portion of the trade in fat stock
which through our not being able to malt
barley, for feeding cattle. is thrown entirely
into the hands of the latter, whereby millions
of acres of good barley land is lost 'to the
country both in England and Ireland, espe-
cially the latter.

7. If these millions of acres were utilised
the price of butchers' meat might fall without
any class feeling, any evil consequences, but
all would undoubtedly feel its benefits, more
especially the lower, and lower -middle classes,
including widows and orphans with limited
fixed incomes.

8. Again, the article in the in con-
clusion says :—.44 The unpalatable truth must
be acknowledged, that the root of agricultural
distress is the found in the redundancy of the
labouring class. Labour may be brought, by
agencies like that started by Canon GIRDLE-
STONE, from a part of the country Where it is
cheap to a part where it is relatively dearer,
but a permanent elevation in the wages of
agricultural labour can be effected only by
limiting the cultivation of the soil to such
proportions as will allow labour to be said with
profit, and by limiting .the army of agricultural
labourers to the number necessary for .tlie cul-
tivation of. tlt area.
0.. And, finally, we-must here enter asolemn
protest against the doctrine promulgated in
the latter part of the above proposition (No. 8)
as a doctrine fraught with economic and
political dangers of a very serious nature, as
tending to bring communism, socialism, and
all other things that follow in the train of
a bloody revolution.

If the Colonial and Indian possessions had
been utilized, and our sons and daughters in
those possessions were cultivating cotton, corn,
wine, oil, and all those things that go to the
feeding and clothing our people, and were
taking British produce and manufacture and
emigrants in exchange, to the same extent the
United States could do if they had no tariffs,
then and not till then may we safely limit our
tilled land; for instance what does it matter, as
far as the interests of our farmers and land-
holders are concerned, whether Dick, Tom,
and Harry, at the Antipodes or Red River
territory, are laying down at their doors
here corn at a certain price per bushel
by their labour, or Dick, Tom, and Harry
at home laying it down at the same doors
by their labour at the same or higher price,
so long as the former process enables the home
land and labour to realise more satisfactory

profits in manufacturing butchers' meat,
fowls, butter, cheese, and milk, and, though last
not least, cheap ...and wholesome beer. Mr.
LOWE by taking off half the duty on coffee,
tacitly admits the unsoundness of these duties;
but who can forgive such tinkering, peddling,
and pettyfogging a policy as half the duty on
coffee being reduced instead of entire repeal,

articles.title: CONTAGIOUS DISEASES ACTS.
articles.text:
THE CONTAGIOUS DISEASES ACTS.

IN your excellent article some time ago on
the subject of Mr. IIItUCE'S proposed Bill fo r
the prevention oil contagious disease, you
pointed out the probability that some snake
might be lurking in its folds. You were
undoubtedly right in this surmise, for the
Bill, while nominally repealing the present
Contagious Diseases Acts, really covertly ex-
tended their iniquitous principles to every
parish in the country, and creates a vast and
permeating officialism for the sole purpose of
getting women under enforced medical control
for immoral purposes. It is not my purpose
just now, however, to disouss the various.
aspects of the bill, but rather, with your per-
mission, to draw attention to the point to
wards which, I believe, that the oonfliot, with
respect to such legislation, is practically
tending. That point may, perhaps, be best
elucidated by quoting a petition which I last
week presented to Parliament in my own
name, through the Right Hon. Mr. STANB-
- It is as follows:

"The petition of the andersigned sheweth,
"That the Bill introduced by Mr. Secretary
Bruce for the prevention of certain contagious
diseases, authorises the surgical violation by men
of the persons of women who are prisoners;
"That your petitioner and other women o this
country, trusting in the help of God, have banded
themselves together to secure that no law shall
over be maintained in peace, which decrees the
surgical violation by men of the persona of women,
under any pretence, by any means, or for any pur-
pose whatsoever. They bold that there is a limit
to what it is lawful for the law to do, and that for
men to invade the most sacred of personal rights
bestowed on women by nature and by God is
an intrinsic wickedness, and can never be made
lawful.

"Therefore your petitioner earnestly prays that
your honourable House will reject any Bill which
authorizes this wickedness, and that no legislation
may hereafter be introduced for the mitigation of
venereal disease, or for the punishment of prosti-
tutes, which does not recognise the inalienable
right of every woman, however mean her station
and however sinful her character, to defend her
person from indecent invasion by mon."
Now, Sir, I appeal to yOu and to your
readers on behalf of the justice of the cry of
outraged womanhood, to which my words in
the above petition are only the dim attempt to
give expression. At every point our aristo-
cratic medical legislators are madly endeavour-
ing to realise these hideous violations of
women. At every point, Sir, we mean to
oppose them, and we shall oppose °them suc-
cessfully. The indignant cry of insulted
womanhood is becoming daily more intense;
it has penetrated within the walls of Parlia-
ment and. is creating anxiety and fear, for our
legislators well know that the final decision
of this question rests with women themselves.
The doctors well know that we have truth and
justice on our side; they well know that GOD
hits bestowed upon the weakest woman the
right to bid any man who wrongs her person
to stand off, even at the peril of his life; they
well know that they are sinning both agaitist
nature and against GOD by these enforced
indecent practiees. The battle about all this
vicious. legislation practically gathers round
this point. It is not, indeed, the limit of our
labours to rid ourselves of the indecent prac-
tices of surgeons; for we have an aim, and Goy
in his providence has a design, far, far, beyond
this—namely, the purification of our national
morality. But I maintain that when once we
shall have succeeded in making doctors keep
their hands off the persons of women, all their
vice-protecting laws and their immunities for
profligacy will fall to pieces; for there is no
violent
,outrage of this kind possible on the
persons of women, which is not directly or
indirectly bound up with some vast fraud
practised on the weaker portion of society by
the stronger, and with some supposed licen-
tious privileges to be won for men.
Certain members of Parliament have lately
been anxiously questioning each other as to
the legality of those outrages which have
lately been so frequently practised on women.
I allude to Such u,,s that in the case of Miss

I Goss, of Herefordshire, who committed suicide
in order to escape violation by the strgeons
who were rattling at her looked door, and
climbing by ladders to her bedroom window;
and I also allude to such as has just recently
been perpetrated on a poor girl at Brighton
(since acquitted. by a jury) on the mere insti-
gation of a policeman. These members of
Parliament, aware that such horrors have
been legalised by the Contagious Diseases
Acts, and, permissively, by the Prison Regu-
lation Act of 1865, are curious to know the
verdict of our older and more decent laws
upon this , subject. The opinion of some of
the elder members of the House was asked;
one of these veterans took "counsel's opinion,"
and the verdict was that such acts arc strictly
illegal. Then, among some of our members of
Parliament, a still deeper anxiety was mani-
fested, and a burning desire by some means
or other to legalise these wicked practices.
Surely in the history of Parliaments no
struggle has ever turned on such a point as
this; surely in succeeding generations the
descendants of the men who passionately
fought in the House of Commons for the right
of indecently violating women will be fain to
hide their heads for very shame. Sir JAMES
MACKINTOSIE said in his defence in the
House of Commons of JOIEN Slim', the
missionary, that the rage of the Jamaica and
Demerara planters against the anti-slavery
party was nothing less than "a rebellion for
the whip." With equal truth we may say
that the present mad determination of our
aristoratio doctors is nothing less than a re-
bellion for the instrumental violation of
woinen. And this conflict is being recorded
on the pages of "Hansard "—a disgraceful,
but yet in some respects a glorious record it
will be; for it will immortalize what women,
aided by the virtuous manhood of England,
will have achieved over an indecent and de-
moralized Legislature over a Legislature
which wantonly violates the first principles of
our constitutional liberty at the bidding of an
insolent medical clique. Dr. SKEY wrote
on February 17th to the Times that it was for
the medical profession, and for that profession
alone, to " dictate " on the subject of the .
Contagious Diseases Acts. Yet this queetieni !
upon which these medical autocrats prestrare 1
to claim the sole right to dictate to this great
nation, and upon which they thus imperiously I
claim the right to shut the mouths of-every
one else, is a question which involves national
morality and purity, and which eonoerns
every citizen of the country. The grate and
serious nature of the constitutional question,
of which medical doctors thus impudently
claim to be sole and irresponsible judges, may
be gathered from the following legal opinion
given by Bir. FILEDINGE GIFFIRD, who was
consulted on the
.subject by the Vigilance
Association. Ile says :—" No trace of the
existence of any such poWer as this order (for
the surgical examination of a woman) assumes,
is to be found in any book of authority; such
an order is contrary to the whole spirit and
principle of our law. I need hardly say that
the law considers all persons innocent till they
are found to be guilty; and further, that the
law invests the person of every one of the
QUEEN'S subjects with its protection against
the merest touch."

I might bring before you in abundance
other proofs of my assertion that our medical
legislators are bent on all hazards on getting
their hands upon women. You will doubtless
have observed the proposal they are at present
urging upon Mr. STANSFELD to create a
medical council with irresponsible powers in
connection with the Local Government Board;
a medical council which would very soon be-
come the tribunal of a great national medical
inquisition.

Without, however, referring to more of such
symptoms, I will conclude by citing the notice
given on the 19th March, in the House of
Commons, by Dr. DONALD DSLUYMPLE, M.P.
for Bath. The notice is to ask Air. BRUCE—
"Whether on account of the frequent instances
of mistakes made in the ease of the execution
of sentence of death on a woman being stayed
on account of the plea of pregnancy, the
ancient custom of the jury of matrons should
not be repealed, and professional experts he
appointed to 4amine a woman in such cir-

cumstanoes." You will observe here-, that
doctors having first expelled women frmu all
opportunity of studying and practising Medi-
cine, take advantage of that faot to Nit fees
into their own pockets. The Vigilance As-
sociation has accordingly drawn up metnbrials
aud petitions as follows :

The humble petition of the undersigned
sheweth—

"That the law providing that a woman under
sentence of death who pleads pregnancy as a bar
to execution shall he examined by a jury of
matrons LS a just, proper, and decent law.
"That it endorses the principle that the inter-
ference of male surgeons with the bodies of Nvomen
is, on no account or under any cireuni4tanees, to
be necessitated by the law of the land,'inttMlnueh
as it protects from Such interference even the body
of a woman condemned to death. .
"That it is a decent and merciful law, mid one
which in its nature involves no Miscarriage of jns-
tice, inasmuch as a jury .of matronsi if properly
elected, are better fitted than any others to deter-
mine as to a case of pregnancy.
"Your petitioners therefore humbly pray that
no alteration May be Made in thisrlaw which 01811
expose a woman condemned to death to. examine-
tion by male surgeons, thereby abolishing a decent
and honourable custom, and stibetituting Itt its
place male eurginal examination of %router!, the
existence of which, enforced by the law of the
land, in any form or under any 'circinnstances, is
an insult to women, a scandal to the medical pro-
fession, and a disgrace to the country.
" Your petitioner's, however, desire to point out
that there is a grave defect in the law ai it at pre-
sent stands, which may lead to miscarritiee of
justice, and which may be very easily remedied.
The defect to which your petitioners allude con-
sists in the custom of empannelling the jury of
matrons from among the women present at the
time in court, inasmuch as the women present on
such occasions are frequently of the lowest and
most ignorant class.
"Your petitioners further beg. to call your
attention to the fact that there now exist in 1,u.g0
numbers women duly qualified to deal fully with
all questions connected with child bearing.
" Your petitioners therefore humbly pray that
your Honourable House will make such an altera-
tion in this law that, while preserving the custom
of the jury of matrons that jury shall henceforth
be empannelled in 'such a way as either to cowist
wholly of duly qualified midwives or to .contain
such in its number."

JOSEPAINE E. BUTLER,
Honorary Secretary to the Vigilance Associa-
tion for the Defence of Pereon4l Itights.

STRIKE AMONG THE AGRICULTURAL
LABOURERS IN WARWICKSIIIRE.

SIGNS of political life and vitality are at
length being manifested by the poor, doWn-
frodden, agricultural labourers, who have been
in a state of semi-serfdom far ages. The'
Obest readers of the BEE-121tvE are aware that
'from the first establishment of that journal, I
have often raised ray voice and called attention
to the miierable poverty-stricken condition or
the agricultural labourers, and have looke I,
and shall continuo to look, with thc deepest
interest to the progress, and as I sincerely hope
the success, of the movement which has now
been so happily commenced and which bids
fair to assume national proportions.

I have reoeived comtnimications front some
of the local leaders in two distliets Where
unions are now being formed, asking for advice
In the formation and hest way of conducting
their union, and if the gentlemen who have
advised the Wantiekshire men in the ethuir-
able and judicious manner they have done, had
been appealed to, their advice Would have
been the same that I have given, With perhaps
this addition, that if it must come to a strike
—which I hope they will try to avoid—they
must be very careful to keep within the pale
of the la*, as the Criminal Law Ametdment
Act, which wasipecially enacted against trades
unionists in towns,would be:applied with equal
rigour against them in the country. I also
pointed out to them not to be too exorbitant
in their demands for any increase or wages
they may demand, and if possible to
get some one to intercede for them, and sub-
mit their claims to arbitration, reminding
them, much in the same language as Professor
BEESLEY in his letter, that it is the landlords
who, in the end, must make up whatever in-
crease of pay they may receive. And this is
what it must and ought to come ; because
any material advance of wages to agricultural
labourers would press with great severity upon
the majority of tenant farmers, as a g„oll
many of them, to use their own homely
phrase, have enough to do to "make ends to
meet." What with the system of raek-rentism
under whieh they live, by which the land-
lords exact the highest Cent they can obtaia
for their land, and the drain upon th,Ar :Tare
means for tazes and rates, they ate hard

Dough pressed in all conscience, and,
as they very truly say, are for the
most part struggling on "from hand to
mouth." Therefore, in endeavouring to in-
crease the wages of agricultural labourers, we
must take into consideration their connection
with their employers, the tenant farmers, and,
again, the connection between the farmers
and their landlords, and when we have done
this, and traced cause and effect, we shall
:discover that before ever the condition of the
agricultural labourer can be materially im-
proved, or the price of their labour raised to
any appreciable extent, the farmers must
either have a reduction of rents to a consi-
derable extent, or hold their farms upon
better conditions and a more favourable
tenure. Thus it will be seen that the first
condition of any real progress in this direc-
tion, must be a considerable alteration of the
tenure by which ,land is held and farmed
in this country. Until this be done all
efforts 'to make any real substantial
or permanent improvement in the condition of
the agricultural labourers will be to a great
extent abortive. Very little will be accom-
plished. by spasmodic efforts of strikes. And
if they did succeed in raising the price of labour
and wages it would have to be at the coat of
the farmers who are. least able to bear it, and
would in no way affect the extortionate rents
paid to landlords. It is the owners of the land,
who give no proportionate return for the enor-
mous rents they receive, that ought to be
called upon to yield up sufficient to improve
the condit.on of the labourers and increase their
rate of wage,. This can only be done by
putting the tenant-farmers and labourers
into the ultimatl possession of the land in
the manner in which it was done in Prussia
under the STEIN system or the Irish Land Act;
or better still, by the mode proposed by the
" Land Tenure Reform Association," of which
Mr. Jourr arta= MILL is chairman. This
Association proposes that the land, as it comes
into the market, shall be bought up by the
Government, the rents accruing therefrom to
be paid into the public Exchequer, and form
part of the public revenue, the same thing to
he done with all waste lands, Now if this was
done, it would prove to be of immense benefit
to the whole community, as well as the agri-
cultural population employed thereon. But
,this cannot be done for some time to come,
and must be preceded by the abolition of the
laws of primogeniture and entail. In the
meantime, if anything can be done to improve
the condition of the agricultural labourers,
by all means let. it be aocomplished. But
what is really wanted is. that there should be
tuition and united action between the tenant-
farmers and the agricultural labourers to
intsist upon an alteration of the conditions
upon which farms are held at present, to en-
-01)10 both labourers and farmers to purchase
farms by availing themselves of the borrowing
powers of an Act of Parliament, which ought
to he passed for Great Britain the same as
the Irish Land Act,

We may all rely upon it that it will have
to come to this at last, and the sooner it
willies the better. This may bo accomplished
without doing the slightest injury or injustice
to the present owners of land, as full com-
pensation would be given them for the land so
purchased. Labourers, as well as farmers,
would then lie able, by thriftiness and in-
dustry, to hare a stake in the country, and
where practicable the introduction of co-
operative farming would greatly assist their
own condition, and increasing the prosperity
of the nation.

LONDON.

STRIKE OF COMPOSITORS.

On Saturday, the fortnight's notice previously
given having expired, the whole of the compositors
employed in the firms of Messrs. Clowes, Judd
and Glass, Kelly, Virtue, Robson, and about a
dozen other large printing establishments struck
work, these firms having, after repeated
interviews with their men, refused compliance
with that part of the memorial sent in by the
compositors claiming an advance of id. per 1,000
letters set up, although several of them were
willing to concede the portion of the memorial
relating to the working hours for the future being
nine per day, or 54 per week. About 150 com-
positors struck 'at Messrs. Clowes's, 100 at Kelly's,
40 at Judd and Glass's, 40 at Robson's, 50 at
Virtue's, 20 at Blanchard's, &c. The aggregate
number of men who struck, comprising the whole
of the compositors employed by the respective
firms, is about 500.
The lists of the turnouts were brought down to
the trade society house in Racquet-court, Fleet-
street, and having been duly verified, the names
were all placed on the books as entitled to receive
strike pay until they obtain employment. The
trade committee express themselves well satisfied
at the almost general acceptance of the terms of
the memorial by the London master printers, con-
sidering that out of about 150 printing firms in
London, not more than sixteen or eighteen have
refused complirnce, and that out of 3,600 members
composing the London Society of Compositors
not more than 600 have been compelled to
strike.

The dissentient employers have been for several
days past advertising in the London and provincial
papers for now hands to fill the places of those
who were going out; while the trade society have
been inserting counter advertisements cautioning
compositors in the country not to seek work in
London while the dispute exists.

Several of the men who left Messrs. Clowes
have been in the employ of the firm thirty and
forty years. The capital stock of the trade
society is about £4,000, but to moot the expenses
of the strike, a levy of 2s. per week is placed
upon every member of the society in work, which,
it is calculated, will produce from £250 to £3OO
per week. The first week's levy was collected on
Saturday last.

The following is taken from the Annual Report

In reviewing the past year, I find it would be

benefit to those seeking employment at these places,
and also to those who are located there. lam de-
sirous that lodges should be opened in every place
where there is a sufficient number of our members
to carry them on.

The increase of members during the year is
very encouraging, being I,722—making a total
of 8,983 at the end of the year. And I
also note with very great pleasure an increase of
£1,804 Bs. 41d. in our accumulated capital—an
increase, I believe, unparalleled in the society's
history in the same space of time—leaving a
balance, on the last meeting night in December, of
£13,974 is. 61d. lam sure this must be cheering
to our members generally; but we must not rest
here. I shall not be satisfied until we have twice
our present number of members, and our accu-
mulated capital increased four-fold. The amount
ol contributions received this year is .£18,250105. 61d.,
being an increase of £3,382 10s. 11)1d. The
amount received for entrances is £1,006 Os. 6d.—
an increase of £4Bl 19s. Bd., or nearly double that
of the previous year. The amount received for
interest on our capital is three times as much as it
was the year before, showing that our banking
accounts have been better attended to by our
lodge trustees. The total income for the year
amounted to £19,614 1 ls. 4d.; to this must be
added £9,169 13s. id., the balance at the com-
mencement of the ye3r—making a total of
£28,784 4s. 6id., an accession of £7,771 17s. 9id.
During the year I find that £4,312 12s. Bd. bas
been paid for sick benefit. £1,377 18s. 3d. has
been paid as superannuation.
We have had four accident claims, amounting to
£240. The amount paid for travelling relief is
£1368 2s. Od. The amount paid as home donation
this year, £lO9 4s. 6d. The surgeons salaries in-
crease in proportion to our members; the sum paid
this ye3r, £1,268 2s. 7d. The amount paid for the
principal benefits of our society during the year is
£11,241, 13s. 7d.
We have paid for benevolent purposes during
the last five years £68,418 2s. .3d., or eight pounds
per member. The amount spent in disputes during
the same period is £2,342, 05.,, or 6s. Oid. per
member compared with the former sum.
I think, in this review of the past year, you will
agree with Me, that we belong to the great army
that is marching onwards; and not only ought we
to be conscious of our own progress, but wisely ob-
servant of the changes happening around us.
Nothing to my mind is more certain, than that we
are now in the process of a great social revolution.
affecting not merely this or that sphere in human
happiness, but touching all the laws under which
we live. Labour begins to think that it may sell
its strength more wisoly. Time never carried such
burdens of events on its shoulders. History never
held in its bosom so many mysteries not yet solved.
Men have never been so busy. Never have so
many questions been stirring and moving men's
minds ; never have the questions themselves been
more various or more vital. Therefore, let us
watch for occasions, that we may seize them ; for
opportunities, that we may improve them; and for
every privilege, that we may embrace them.
I am, yours faithfully,
K. KNIGHT, C. Sec.
General Office, 26, Russell-street,
Liverpool, March Ist. 1872.

articles.title: TILE LIBOUILE
articles.text:
TILE LIBOUILE

Since Saturday last, upwards of 100 men em-
ployed in constructing the new tunnel in Groat
George-strest, Liverpool, for the Cheshire Lines
Railway, which will connect the line from Bruns-
wick station with the new station now in course
of erection in Ranelagh-strect, have been on strike
for a reduction of the hours of labour, and the
works are almost at a Eitand4till. The men have
been accustomed to work from 6 a.m. to 6
two hours of the time being allowed for meals ;
but they now contend for eight hours per day, in.
eluding half an hour for dinner.

NORWICH.
TUE CARPENTERS AND JOINERS.

Sir,—l nave watched your valuable paper with
the expectAtion of seeing some account of our
agitation and strike. As I have not, if it meet

with your approval to publish, I will furnish
you with a short account. We sent a circular
from the SOciety to the Masters, after taking
the opinion of the whole trade, to the following
effect: That our time be reduced from 59 to 54
hours, with id. per hour extra, and Id, per hour
extra for overtime, and time and a half for Satur-
day after one o'clock; to which we received no
reply, followed by two reminders with the same
effect. Consequently a large meeting at the Bell
Hotel took place, at which it was adopted, for
the convenience of the Masters, that the time be
661 hours, and that a circular be sent to the
Masters, giving notice that the men would leave
work on the first Monday in March, if their
requests were not acceded to, which was carried
into effect, and we have been on strike over
since. About three-fourths turned out; the re-
mainder kept at work.—Remaining yours respect-
fully, ALFRED JOHNSON'.

articles.title: BIR NI INGHAM. TIIE BRICEMAKEES.
articles.text:
BIR NI INGHAM.
TIIE BRICEMAKEES.

At a general meeting of operative brickmakers
held at the Sportsman, Garrison-lane, Birming-
ham, it was resolved that the moulders should
have what they asked for in their last request,
and day men accept the offers of the employers as
to the increase of wages, providing the nine hours
is conceded ; kiln work to be advanced in propor-
tion. All work is to cease until the above terms
are conceded.

A conference was bold on Thursday between

were fatly discussed. As a mutual understanding
has been comet°, subject to the approval of a trade
meeting, it has been agreed to ask the men on

articles.text:
CORK.

TIIE COACIIMAKEItIe LOCK-OUT.
The coaehmakers of Cork are now " looked out"

LEEDS.

THE TRADES COUNOIL AND THE MASTER AND

SERVANTS (WAGES) BILL.

The following replies have been received to
letters sent by the Leeds and District Trades'
Council to the borough and county members,
requesting them to support the Master and Ser-
vants (Wages) Bill, now before the House of
Commons :

"25, Ebury-street, London, March 15, 1872.
"Dear Sir,-1 hope to be in my place in the
House of Commons when the bill to which your
letter refers comes on for discussion. I think it
is a very good bill, and shall give it my support.
—Yours truly, "It. M. CARTE%
"Mr. Thomas Packett."

"My dear Sir,—l am obliged by your nom.
munication having (I suppose) reference to the
Government Bill as to Master and Servant.

"I say I suppose,' because that is the sole
bill now before us that deals with the law as to
the payment of wages.
"I can assure you that this measure will have
my most devoted attention, the more especially as
I have been, ever since I was a boy, most strongly
impressed with the absolute necessity of paying
wages in current coin, and in current coin only, so
as to enable us to got rid of the possibility of
fraud, and (if I may use any expression so strong)
the abominations of the truck system.
"If, as I take it to be, this is the principle you
ask me to support, I tell you, without the slightest
reserve or the least hesitation, that I shall do so
to the fullest possible extent in my power. If I
be right, too, in the idea that this is the bill to
which your letter refers, in other respects, though
I think the measure may receive some alterations
when in committee, I think its object very useful
taken as a whole.—Yours faithfully,
"W. Sr. J. WuEELnousE."

"21st March, 1872.

" Sir,—T bog to acknowledge the receipt of
your note of the 16th instant, with copy of petition
which you purpose to send to the House of Com-
mons.

"There are several parts of the Master and
Servants Wages Bill with which I do not agree—
such as compelling masters to pay wages once a
week, and authorising the payment of sums above
£6 in cheque on bankers
in
consent of work-
men), and which I shall, n committee, endeavour
to amend; but in all that relates to the payment
of wages in the current coin of the realm, and the
abolition of the truck system, the bill has my
cordial support.
I cannot support any bill to repeal the criminal
clauses of the Master and Workmen Act passed
last session. Those clauses apply equally to the
masters as well as to the workmen, and are, in my
opinion, absolutely necessary to prevent oppression
by masters over workmen, and by combination of
Workmen over their fellow-wtirkers.—l am, sir,
your obedient servant, " JOSItUA FIELDEN.
"Mr. Thomas Plackett."

articles.title: STRIKES.
articles.text:
THE STRIKES.

THE PELT TRAMIL—The felt operatives have,
after a month's strike for the nine hours limit,
agreed to return to work on the old terms.

-Tun FLAX TnAnn—At a mass meeting of the
flax operatives, hold on Wednesday afternoon, to
consider whether the masters' offer of an advance
of wages should bo accepted, or whether there
k)hould be a further stand for tho nine hours' limit
the chairman (Mr. Kendall) said the rumour that
the strike was about to end was a "dodge " . of
the masters to stop subscriptions. Only at two
mills had the men given way; the hands at other
places remained firm. lie believed that if they
remained united a while longer they must achieve
success. A resolution was unanimously adopted,
pledging the meeting to remain firm to the " nine
hours," and to accept no compromise. At a second
meeting hold subsequently a similar resolution
Nes enthusiastically carried. It was stated that
the ongirleers, iron-makers, and other trades had
resolved to sopport the strike hands.

MANCHESTER.
VIE GILDING TRADE.

Bir,-.-The success which has attended the agita-
tion in connection with the above-mentioned
trade in Manchester has prompted us to respect-
fully ask you to allow us space in your columns of
Trades Intelligence, to enable us to gain as wide-
spread publicity to the movement as possible, be-
lieving that your journal has very great circula-
tion amongst all classes of workmen, and will,
therefore, stimulate to action those in our own
trade who have not up to the present time given
very little or no attention to tho question. The
expense attending the agitation in Manchester has
been of so slight a character as to scarcely need
mentioning—a fact arising, we have no doubt
whatever, from the judgment and foreeiglit which
enabled Afr. Chas. Rowley, carver and gilder,
Bond-street, Manchester, to take the precedence
by at once granting the concession desired by the
Workmen in his employ, and while we congratulate
ourselves that the inevitable result hasbeen attained
at so little cost, we feel grateful to those whose
Bympathy would have become an active feature in
the agitation had it assumed the appearance of
becoming prolonged. We may also state that,
While on our part the attitude has been respectful,

we have received throughout the courteous atten-
tion of the employers.—We remain respectfully,
HFNRY Gun:um, Treasurer.
Mr. BRIDGEMAN, Chairman.
Mr. Jonx Swxxnum, Secretary.
United Framemakers and Gildors Asso-
ciation to promote the reduction of the
hours of labour.
Saddle Inn, Blackfriars-street, Salford.

The undermentioned firms have adopted the
nine hours system in Manch'ester :—Mr. Charles
Rowley, Bond-street, Oldham-road; Mr. jarnes

articles.title: COVENTRY.
articles.text:
COVENTRY.

THE BUILDING OPERATIVES.

At Coventry, an increase of wages of operatives
in the building trade came into operation on the
2nd of April. Notices from the carpenters and
joiners having been issued to the masters for an
advance of three farthings per hour upon the
present rate, viz., from sid. to 60. per hour
from the bricklayers for an advance of one half-
penny per hour, from 6d. to 60., and from the
labourers for an advance of one halfpenny
per hour, from 33d. to 4td. This advance
the masters could not accede to; therefore :the
question was submitted to arbitration for settle-
ment. The carpenters and joiners appointed Mr.
W. 11. Hill, mayor; and the bricklayers and
labourers, Mr. J. Gulson. Both these gentlemen
kindly consented to act, and after having the
matter laid before them by the delegates appointed
they have given in their award as follows
The carpenters and joiners to have 60. per hour,
being a rise of 2s. 11d. per week of 56i hours,
that is from 275. Id. to 305.; the bricklayers Cal
per hour, being a rise of Is. 9d. per week, from
28s. 3d. to 305.; and the labourers 4d. per hour
being a rise of Is. 2d. per week, from 17s. Bd. to
18s. 101, and all overtime, made at the request of
the master, between eight o'clock in the evening
and six o'clock in the morning, to be paid for at
the rate of time and half. Overtime to commence
on Saturdays at one o'clock, and on Sundays
double the ordinary rate to be paid. Overtime
for labourers to commence at four o'clock on
Saturdays as before.

GLOUCESTER.
TIIE BUILDING TRADES.

The operatives in the Gloucester building trades
have met near the Park, opposite the Whitfield
Memorial Church, now being completed, to con-
sider the answer given by the masters to their demand
for the adoption of the nine hours' movement, after
the fashion of most of the other large works in the
city. Two of the masters had sent letters saying
that they would adopt the system if others in the
trade did the like, and a third offered to concede
part of the demand, and the remainder in time to
come, after certain large works now proceeding
had been completed. But the men, gathered in
crowd in the rain, unanimously resolved that they
would accept nought less than their full demand,
and then dispersed. It was understood that, if
their request were not granted, they would strike.

REDDITCH.
TIIR BUILDING TUADE.

The whole of the carpenters, bricklayers, and
painters employed at Redditch haVe struck this
week in consequence of their demands not being
acceded to. The carpenters and bricklayers
require a rise in their wages of Is. per week, and
to leave off work at one o'clock on Saturdays; and
the painters demand an increase of 2s. per week,
besides the diminished hours on Saturdays.

articles.title: LEICESTER.
articles.text:
LEICESTER.

THE CARPENTEUS.

On Monday, about 300 carpenters of Leicester
struck for shorter hours and increased pay. The
masters have offered to submit the matter to arbi-
tration, and though during the course of the nego-
ciations the men accepted arbitration, they now
refuse, and have struck to enforce their demands.
The workmen in the brickfields around hero are
on strike for an advance of 4d. per thousand in the
making, and other departments in proportion. The
master builders have resolved, in the event of the
stone masons not accepting 71d. per hour, and Bd,
for public jobs, to require six months' notice from
Ist April, and have framed other regulations in
reference to bricklayers and labourers. They also
pledge themselves to support one another in carry-
ing out those regulations.

ST. HELEN'S.

AMALGAMATED MINERS' ASSOCIATION CONFERENCE.

A conference of miners was opened on Tuesday
at St. Helen's. Mr. Thomas Halliday, president
of the Amalgamated Association, was in the
chair.

The following places were represented by dole
gates :—Wigan, Farnworth, and Kersley, Woreley.
St. Helen's, Hollinwood Church, North Stafford-
shire, South Staffordshire, North Wales, Rhondda
Valley, Aberdare, Abertillery, , Caerphilly, Merthyr
Tydvil, Forest of Dean, 'West Gloucester, and
Bristol.

The President, in opening the conference, said
the meeting was the most momentous that had
ever been held in connection with a branch of
industry second to none in the kingdom in point of
importance.

The business of examining credentials, fixing
the hours of sittings, and arranging a series of
public meetings in the neighbourhood, having
been disposed of, the meeting proceeded to con-
sider applications for the creation of now districts,
and, after considerable discussion, new districts in
communication with the association were allowed
to be elected in Cannock Chase, Stafford, Abera-
von (Wales), and Neath (Wales). An application
from Blaenavon for a similar privilege was refused.
Arrangements were made to hold public meetings
in Haydock, Thatto Heath, Ashton rarr, and
Whiston. There was a largo tea meeting in the
evening in the Volunteer Hall.

WEDNESDAY.—Tho business of this conference
at St. Helen's was resumed on Wednesday, Mr.
Halliday presiding.
The financial position of the districts was re-
ported to be satisfactory.
The chairman then delivered an address, in
course of which he congratulated the meeting on
the success which had attended the association
daring its three years' existence. A firm foothold
had been obtained in Lancashire, Staffordshire,
and North and South Wales, and through the
agency of the association working miners had
secured advances in wages from 25 to 30 per cent.
The object of the agitation on the wages question
was to go back to the wages of 1867, and,
nominally, they had succeeded; but in some
instances, the coal owners, while putting on 3s. a
ton to the consumer, had not carried out their
promises to the workmen. The association corn-
prised 26,000 members—an increase of 10,000 in
six months—and £1,314 was in bank, as against
£362 six moßths ago. Adverting to Parlia-
mentary matters, he characterised Mr. Bruce's bill
as an honest effort to meet the wishes of the
miners generally; but he declared his conviction
that they should never be sqtisfied uutil they had
a direct representative in Parliament.

District reports were then presented, showing
much progress in the movement for lessening the
hours of labour and obtaining advanced wages.

articles.title: NORTHAMPTON. TIER BUILDING TRADE.
articles.text:
NORTHAMPTON.
TIER BUILDING TRADE.

At a mass meeting of building operatives, bold
at the Royal Hotel, Gold-street. Northampton, on
Thursday, the 28th of March, 1872, the following
resolutions were unanimously passed
"1. That the memorial to the employers asking
that 6d. per hour be paid, and 54 hours constitute
the week, be adhered to. •

"2. That notice be given to the employers that,
unless the terms offdrel in the memorial be ac-

articles.title: STA.FFORSHIRE. AGITATION AMONGST COLLICRS.
articles.text:
STA.FFORSHIRE.
AGITATION AMONGST COLLICRS.

On Tuesday a conference of miners' delegates,
representing 9,000 colliers, was held in Dudley, to
consider the present condition of the trade. It
was pointed out that men in other districts were
enjoying greater privileges in the way of shorter
hours than the South Staffordshire colliers, and it
was -agreed to form a great union of the old and
new lists of South Staffordshire districts on the
basis of the Northern societies. This was agreed
to on the ground that a union would gain the
coveted privileges easier than by single exertion.
The meeting was most successful.

articles.title: WARWICKSUIRE. FARM LABOUREIte STRIICE.
articles.text:
WARWICKSUIRE.
FARM LABOUREIte STRIICE.

We received last week, too late for publication,
the following sums for the support of farm
labourers on strike :—Members of London BRE-
ITIvE Lodge Carpenters, 108. ; A few Members,
ditto, 148. 10(1. ; Smith and Taylor's Joiners, Bs. ;
Olemence's Joiners' Shop, Lambeth, 4s. Id.
The above has been sent to Mr. Taylor, at

This week vre have received Smith and

Society Carpenters, 9s. 11d.

WEDNESDAY.--At a meeting of the oxecutivis
committee of the Warwickshire Labourers' Union,
held at the Regent Hotel, Leamington, on Tues-
day night, Mr. Auberon
‘llerbert presiding, Mr.
Arch was appointed organising secretary, at a
salary of 21s. weekly; and Mr. Russell, secretary,
at the same remuneration; both exclusive of
travelling expenses. The following wages were
adopted :—Able-bodied labourers 53. a day and no
beer in harvest; inefficient men to be engaged at
lower rates; all such bargains to be made by the
men working under the same employer. The
wages in ordinary times to be Ns. the week of 91.
hours per day.

BIRMINGHAM, THURSDAY NIGHT.

The movement for improving the condition of
the farm labourers has been taken up heartily
in Birmingham, and a Yarge and influentially
attended mooting was held at the Town Hall on
Wednesday night, for the purpose of giving the
labourers substantial assistance. Mr. J. S.
Wright, chairman of the Birmingham Liberal
Association, presided, and the attendance included
several loading townsmen. Very liberal subscrip-
tions wore promised. One gentleman, besides
giving £2O, offered a week for ton or twelv
weeks, and the chairman promised £3 a week for
a like time. Mr. Arch, the " apostle "of the
movement, addressoi the meeting and was well
received. Oa the motion of Dr. Langford,
seconded by the Rev. It. W. Dale, it was resolved
—"That in the opinion of this meeting the condi-
tion of the agricultural labourers is a reproach to
civilisation, and that the present efLrts of the
men in South Warwiekshiro to improve their
condition deserves its hearty sympathy and sup-
port." A committee was formed.

articles.title: DUNDEE.
articles.text:
DUNDEE.

TIIE NINE MOUES MOVEMENT.
On Tuesday night, in terms of a circular issuol
by the delegates who have charge of the move-
ment in .Dundoe for agitating the reduction of the
working hours of ironworkers in factories and
mills to fifty-one per week, a conference was held,
but no representative of the employers attended
the meeting. It was stated that some of the
masters had agreed to grant the request of the
men on the Ist of June, when the fifty-one hours'
system is to begin in the ironfoundries in the
town. Some of the speakers suggested that a
strike should be resolved on at once, but it was
ultimately agreed to call a mass meeting of the
men before taking any definite stops in the
matter.

articles.title: MONTRESL.
articles.text:
MONTRESL.

TILE NINE ROUES ILOVEUENT.

A general meeting of working men interested in
the nine hour movement was held last night, in
Perry's Hell, Craig-street. The ()heir was occupied
by Mr. Wm. Moore. The meeting WAS opened at
eight o'clock by the chairman, who gave a short
report of the proceedings of a -previous meeting,
whore delegates were present from 23 establish-
ments in the city, who represented that about 12
firms had consented to grant the desired concession,
He also stated that it was desired to make the
movement more general and embrace all trades
within it. Mr. Black, of the Grand Trunk works,
then addressed the mooting, urging that the
movement should be more general. He instenced
the progress of the movement in England and
Scotland, and spoke of the meetings which had
recently taken place in Hamilton. What they
demanded was an increase of ten per cent. on their
wages, and that, instead of being paid in money,
they should be paid in time, which they could
devote to recreation and the improvement of their
intellects. The men of Hamilton wore to turn out
on the lath of May, and if their demand were not
granted, then the tuen of Montreal should be pre-
pared to assist them. He moved that a society be
formed to be named the Montreal -Union Lebour
League. After this motion had boon put several
speeches were made, and seven delegates from
different establishments reported. Four out of the
seven had the consent of their employers to the
scheme, two were unfavourable, and one would
not give his opinion until he had consulted with
other employers. The motion was then adopted.

• TORONTO.
Tun NINE HOURS MOVEMENT.

The workmen of the iron trades in Toronto held
a mass meeting in that city on Saturday night, for
the purpose of discussing this question. Aldermen
Dickey and Canavan were present and delivered

short speeches* exprosalng themselves mush grati-
fied et tile agitation of the matter. At the cow.
clioion of the meeting the "Toronto Xrou Short-
Time League " was formed, and stops were taken
for the pnrpose of acting in concert with other
trade unions, and spreading the agitation through
evcry town and city of the Dominion.

articles.title: MISCELLANEOUS TRADES.
articles.text:
MISCELLANEOUS TRADES.

ADDRESS OF THE EXECUTIVE OF
THE AUALGFAMATED SOCIETY OF
TAILORS.
TO TUN OFERATIVE TAILOILS 01' THE UNITED

ICINGDONI.

GENTLEMEN,—We again address you, in the
interest of that unity so essentially necessary for
our well-being as a trade, and of enlisting your
sympathies, co-operation, and help, in the strenuous
efforts now being made for the moral and social
regeneration of our occupation, to the end that all
may be partakers in the good work that is to be
accomplished.
Our object -is not to take undue advantage of
any town, place, or person, but, by strong and
powerful unity, secure to ourselves the advan-
tages of the improved trade of the country, and
by gradual, prudent, and continuous efforts, regain
the position lost during the first forty years for
want of unity, that we may keep pace with our
fellow-tradesmen throughout the country, and
share in the general benefits gradually gained by
working men through their mile ns.
The nature and objects of our union have been,
and still are, very much misunderstood and misre-
presented; and we desire, as far as in our ability
lies, to clear away that misapprehension, and to
state definitely what we consider to be the legiti-
mate objects of our association, and to vindicate
our rights and character as a trade.

As a friendly society organised for mutual help
in sickness, superannuation, and death, we occupy
a proud position. Since the commencement of
our present rules our Association offers the widest
possible basis for the unity of the trade consistent
with due payment of benefits held forth.

Wo have expended in benevolent objects of our
society since the inauguration of our present rules,
May Ist, 1869, to December 31st, 1871—

Sick donation
Travelling relief to members
seeking employment
Funeral donation 1733 3 5

Total
During the past year, for the same purposes—

Funerals of members and mem-
bers' wives
Travelling relief to members
seeking employment

Total for past year alone.. £2925 4 3
And with the above we have appended the fol-
lowing paragraph from the Auditors' Report of
the past year :
"On a careful review of this report, it will be
seen that 1871 has boon the most successful year
that we have had since the commencement of the
Society—from the first quarter to the last there
being an increase of nearly; 1,000 members, and
au increase in the funds of £1,114 10s. Old. ; the
total worth of the Society being £2,374 10s. lid.,
or an average of 10s. per member, a result that
must be highly gratifying to the members, as at
once showing the sound financial position of our
undertaking."
Therefore, with these facts before us, and the
knowledge that even with the failure of our
greatest effort, we have been enabled to place the
wages question of our trade in such a position that
it never occupied before, and are at the present
moment engaged in acquiring still further benefits
in this direction, we therefore solicit the whole
trade to form under our banner and become
branches of the great tree of amalgamation.
PETER SHORROCITH, Secretary.
