IMPORTANT DgcISION.

REATBLEY V. TUSTIN.

This WAS a claim of £1 10s., brought by the
plaintiff, formerly a coach body-maker at. Messrs.
Hallam's, Worcester, but now of London, against
the defendant, a farmer, living at Itonkswood,
near 'Worcester.

Mr. Meredith appeared for the plaintiff, and
Mr. Clutterbuck for the defendant.

It appeared from the evidence that in Septem-
ber last the defendant's son went to Messrs.
Hallam's shop to learn the trade, awl the plain,
tiff (who was working on piece) allowed him to
UBO his tools for seven weeks, and also spent several
hours in going to Messrs. Hull's to buy now ones for
him. For this Mr. Tustin promised to pay plain-
tiff, • but as he had since refused, to pay, this
action was brought. Defendant paid Os. into
court previous to the hearing of the case. The
plaintiff and a witness named Spooner swore
that 30s. was a very low sum for the damage
done to the tools and the time wasted in going
to Messrs. Hall's. In answer to Mr. Clutter.
buck, the former said that he had very often to
undo the work done by the lad, and his work
was pro Riess.

Ma Honour asked Mr. Meredith whether be
could not bring evidence of a more conclusive
nature. The plaintiff might as well have claimed

Mr. Meredith replied that the case would have
to rest on this, as there was no particular rule
in the trade. He called, however, Gaorgo Budd,
who said be was a coachbuilder, swore
that it was the custom for the apprentices to
bring their own tools, or pay the man for the
tools they borrowed. In answer to his Honour,
witness stated that if a tramp had a job ho
would have to allow his employer ss. a week
for the use of tools.

His Honour said the real gist of this action was
a problem which for years he had been trying to
solve; he had not yor arrived at a satisfactory
conclusion, viz., the injustice which allows a
master to take a premium with an apprentice and
then throw him upon a skilled workman who got
nothing for his trouble of teaching him. The
very intelligent manner in which CI. Budd had
given his evidence materially helped him to arrive
at a decision.

Mr. Cluttorbuck submitted that tho plaintiff
was coming by a sidowind on the apprentice's
father to pay for those tools which ought to be
provided by the master. He called Mr, Hallam,
who said that the plaintiff had the benefit of the
work dono by the lad,
In answer to Mr. Meredith, witness said that
the lacl would be very useful in many ways to the
plaintiff.
Mr. Tustin, the defendant, swore that he
never offered to pay the plaintiff for the use of the
tools. He offered to pay him for the time he lost
in going to Messrs. Hall's.
The son of the defendant was called, and ad-
milted that he used the plaintiff's tools. He
believed that the plaintiff did his best to teach
him the trade.

His Honour, in giving a verdict for the plaintiff
with costs, said, that the evidence of James Tustin
clearly showed to him that the services rendered
by the plaintiff could not be estimated sim ply by
the loss of time, for the skill and judgment proved
to have been exercised in the selection of new
tools had saved defendant a considerable sum of
money, the very lowest sum he could name was
that which plaintiff had asked, 30s. and costs.

CO-OPERTATI'VE CONGRESS AT

BOLTON.

The fourth annual congress of the members of
the co.operative societies of England was opened
in the Co-operative Hall, Bolton, on Monday
morning. There was a large attendance of dele-
gates. Mr. Thomas Hughes, M.P., presided.
The Chairman, in delivering the inaugural
address, said that they met this year with unpre-
cedented success. In the majority of stores
throughout the country 2s. in the pound had been
returned to the members as bonus. He sYosPa"
thised to a great extent with the anxiety an 4 dis-
tress of the struggling retail trader who saw the
co-operative system carrying off his custom, but
the way to meet the danger was met by such
arguments as the Chamber of Trade put forth.
Let them rather take a leaf out of their rivals'
book. The three watchwords of the co-operative
movement bad been "pure goods," "just mea-
sures," "cash payments." Referring to the land
question, the President said that by the Mt
passed last session, through the instrumentality of
Mr. Morrison, they had practically more powers
in dealing with real property than building
societies; but still let them not be in A hurry to
lock up too much of their spare capital in land or
houses. The working men of this country were
just now stricken with the land fever. Ito was
glad of it; the fonder they were of English soil,
the better for England; but their societies would
hinder that if they went too fast. Let them
remember that they were trading bodies, and
liable at any time to large calls on their business
transactions. Mr. Hughes also advised all so-
cieties to convert the whole of their capital into
transferable shares. Societies which did this could
not suffer by any merely temporary embarrass.
ment. Mr. Hughes went on to speak highly of
the educational power which lay under the co-
operative movement.
Mr. Rutherford (Newcastle) proposed a vote of
thanks to Mr. Hughes for an address which
was pregnant with thought, and formed a fitting
opening to so important a congress.
Mr. Lloyd Jones (London) seconded the proposi-
tion, and said they would all feel grateful to Mr.
Hughes for the earnest advocacy he had given to
the cause of co-operation for so many years.
The motion was adopted by acclamation.

The report of the Central Board, which was
very lengthy, was lead by Mr. Pare, honorary
secretary. It spoke of the steadily increasing hi

gressess since their institution in London in 1869.

England Co-operative Wholesale Society. The
number of societies in federation had increased
during the year from 209 to 235, whilst the
societies supplied with goods had increased from
345 to 390. The capital had also increased front
£44,000 to upwards of £52,000, and the quarterly'
turnover, which a year ago was £160,000, Was
last quarter £200,000. The disposable net profit
for the year was £7,869, the sales having been
£758,761. The branch establishment at Newj

the end of the first three months the goods sup-
plied to the stores in the four northern counties
were £25,000, being an increase of 64 per cent.
over the corresponding period of the previous
year. The Wholesale Soceiety had also opened
up a connection with many continental houses for
the supply of provisions and clothing. Since the
passing of the amended Industrial Societies Mt
numerous co-operative societies had entered some"
what extensively into cottage building. je con
-
elusion, the report alluded to tho question of
organisation and propaganda, and said the co-
operative movement had now attained such ditnon-
sions as to have sensibly affected the interests of
the ordinary shopkeepers, who, alarmed at the
prospect before them, had assumed an attitude of
attack. It therefore behoved the co-operators to
close their ranks, and by a thorough organisation
be the better prepared to withstand any assaults
which might be made on the movement or if
more prominent friends.
The adoption of the report was moved by gr.
G. J. Holyoak e, seconded by Mr. Barr (ales'
gow), and adopted.
Mr. E. 0. Greening (Manchester) read a paper,
on "Co-operative societies combining for mutua.l
.guarantee." A long discussion ensued, when
it
was resolved to collect statistics with" t vie° ta
test the probability of mutual guarantee amongst
co-operative societies.
Mr. Greenwood deliverel an address on ITIIO
best system to modify the present plan of with-
drawing capital subscribed on shares," and movca
a resolution, the effect of which s as recommending
the matter for further consideration in local socie-
ties.
After a long discussion, this proposition wag

agreed to on a division, the numbers being 5; for,
and six against. _ _ _

Dr. Rutherford (Newcastle) then delivered an
address on the propriety of forming a co-operative
bank, and at the conclusion of his remarks the

TvEsDAY.—The Co-operative Congress was re-
sumed this morning. A letter was read from Mr.
Hughes, M.P., stating that he could not attend on
account of the death of Mr. Maurice, whom he
regarded as the best and wisest Englishman he had
ever known.

Papers on the prevention of fraud and the check
system baying been read, it was resolved, on the
motion of Mr. Lloyd Jones, of London, seconded
by Mr. Holyoalce, also of London—" That, whilst
experimenting in effective checking be continued
and compared with a view to improvement in that
respect, this Congress recommends to the various

The following places were proposed at which to
hold the next congress :—Hookmondwike, New-

"That the Central Board be requested to collect

articles.title: NATIONAL INFLUENOE.
articles.text:
NATIONAL INFLUENOE.

There is a kind of influence which England
may, and, we believe, in largo measure does,
exercise over the nations, which we must all desire
to see maintained and extendel to the utmost. It
is the influence she can exert by her religion, her
philanthropy, her literature, her commerce, and,
above all, her example. The example which Eng-
land offers to other countries, of institutions in
which the problem of combining liberty and order
luts,-lin some degree at least, been solved; the
example of growing 'prosperity, of peaceable pro-
gresss, of great activity in works of chant y and
mercy, and, we will add, the example she has
given of minding her own business, without
meddling in other men's affairs, and reaping
the reward of her abstinence by saving
her blood ;and treasure all this cannot
fail to tell powerfully upon surrounding nations,
if we leave that iufluenee to its natural operation,
without attempting to force ourselves obtrusively
and offensively upon them. But this is by no means
what too many even of our leading statesmen
mean by "influence." What they want is something
laud, aggressive, dictatorial, menacing, the influence
that is to be sustained by an officious and swagger-
ing diplomacy, and by having a large army and
navy in the background to threaten and command.
"English influence abroad" was one of the con-
juring phrases with which Lord Palmerston
so long deluded his countrymen; and the
idea it embodies, if it can be said to
embody any idea, formed the corner stone of
that meddling and mischievous policy by which,
without in any appreciable degree affecting the
current of European affairs, he made the name of
England hated all over the world. No better way
could be taken to bring into discredit this vile
phrase than by tracing its effects when reduced to
action by Lord Palmerston. Wo have not the
time or space to do it now very fully. But we
refer to a few illustrative facts. In 1840 he used
the influence of England to form the Quadruple
Treaty, the only effect of which was to deliver
Syria over to a much worse ruler than we had
to depose, and to bring us to the very verge of a
war with France, from which we wore only saved
probably by the timely succession of Lord Aber-
deen to office. 111 1849 he used the influence of
England to pick another quarrel with France on
the question of Spanish marriage 3, on which the
events that immediately followed formed so bitter
an ironical comment. In 1848 ho used the in-
fluence of England to encourage an insurrection
in Sicily, and then withdrew his protection,
leaving the unfortunate Sicilians t) the tender
mercies of the King ef Naples. In 1860 the
pretext of upholding English influence led him to
that quarrel with, and attack upon, the little king-
dom of Greece, which. excited the execration of
all nations, brought upon him and upon us a
humiliating lecture from Count Nesselrode, and a
great increase of Russian influence in the East of
Europe, led to that breach of faith with the
French Government• which issued in the recall of
the French Ambassador from London, and to such
exasperation of feeling throughout France as
probably would have led to war if their hands
had not been full with the business of re-organ-
ising their own Government after the Revolution.
And so we might go on with e succession of
events in which the "influence of England" was
put forth as an excuse for a policy of intervention,
the principal effect of which was to irritate the
governments of Europe against us, and to betray
the people who had trusted us.

articles.title: MR. DISRAELI AT MANCHESTER.
articles.text:
MR. DISRAELI AT MANCHESTER.

An immense audience assembled in the
Free-trade Hall on Wednesday night to hear
from the lips of the Conservative chief an
exposition of the principles upon which the
further progress of the "tide of democracy "
is to be stemmed. The doors of the hall were
besieged two hours before the commencement
of the proceedings; and Mr. Disraeli, on
arriving in view of the crowd that blocked up
Peter. street, was received with an outburst of
enthusiasm. Inside the hall the scene was one
that might have inspired a great orator, like
Mr. Bright, or Mr. Gladstone, to an effort
worthy of his fame. Mr. Disraeli found
himself in the ball where his greatest rivals
have achieved some of their most remarkable
succeeses. An audience densely packed upon
platforms, floor, and galleries received him
with a roar of applause, the swelling strains of
the organ rolled grandly forth, and the
enthusiasm of the -vast meeting culmi-
nated when the first notes of the
" National Anthem " burst upon the
ear. Mr. Disraeli stood calm and im-
passable, as is his wont, surveying the
crowd with a •quiet scrutiny, until the
"Kentish fire," the strains of "God save the
Queen," the shouting, and the clapping of
hands, gradually subsided. His first sen-
tenees contained a becoming allusion to his
former visits to Manchester, when he presided
over gatherings of the members of the
Athenteum and. the Mechanics' Institution.
He then alluded with a triumphant air
to the splendid welcome he had received
at the Pomona Gardens from "representa-
tives of all the divisions of Lancashire,"
and in the next few sentences, loftily conceived
and delivered with great spirit, lie led the
audience to believe that they were about at
once to learn all about the mysterious "Con-
servative programme." The Liberals, he said,
had told the county that the Conservatives had
no programme. Well, he ventured—and here,
with consummate art, Mr. Disraeli spoke in a
tone of studied humility—as one who was
honoured by the confidence of the Conservative
party, and who came forward at the invitation
of Lancashire, to tell them what that pro-
gramme was. The hall resounded with cheers;
but Mr. Disraeli went on to say rather what
his programme was not than what it was.
His sentences had a familiar ring to students
of his speeches in the House. Ils would not
pursue a policy of despoiling churches and
plundering landlords; he would. not menace
every institution and. every class; but—and
these words were spoken with slow and deli-
berate emphasis, and in Mr. Disraeli's most
sonorous voice—" a policy which had distinct
aims, which was deeply concerned with the
interests of the great body of the people," that
was the policy end the programme which he
was prepared, on that platform and elsewhere,
to assort and to vindicate' as "one not un-
worthy of those with whom he acted in poli-
tical life." Summing 4p his policy in a single
phrase, he declared it to be "the same and
unchangeable"—Queen, Lords, and Commons.
Mr. Disraeli enlarged with an evident relish
for the subject upon the advantages of which
"the Throne" has secured for the nation,
and he treated with scorn the attacks which
had been made upon the monarchy on the
ground of expense. He contrasted the sove-
reignty of the United Kingdom with the

the Congress which meets at Washington to
the pay and allowances of the various State

triumphantly to figures which proved that the
amount of the English Civil List was very
sawn indeed when compared with the sums
absorbed by the governing bodies in the States.
The best "hits' of the speech were made on
this subject; and a hearty cheer was the re-
sponse to his emphatic assertion that there was
no sovereignty in the world so cheap—" for
be would use the mean epithet "—as
the sovereignty of the British Empire. He

enthusiasm" Which the " Republicans of 131r-
iningliam ' had exhibited on this subject, and

here was a shout of applause and laughter

progress of reform. He complained that the

step through the familiar path which landed
them at the Reform Act of 1887, when for the

best manner, Mr. Disraeli contrasted the con-
dition of England in 1849, when revolution
was raging in France, with the spirit in which
the Communal revolt was met. In the first

tone) "there was a day when no women
dared to leave her house in London, and when
artillery was planted on Westminster Bridgu ;"
but in 1871, although the rod flag was
displayed in Paris, "you could not got
tive men in London or Manchester to
meet together and grumble." And why ?
Because the working 'pealed got their rights
and were content. They were more; they
were grateful. Mr. Morten revived the
waning enthusiasm of the meeting by an
enlogy upon the blessings that .flow naturally
from a State Church, or, as lie phrased it, " the
irrestimable blessings of a pnblic reeognition
of religion by the State." This naturally led
him to the eduoation question, and he declared
that the Nonoonformists had equal advantages
with Churchmen under the Education Act.
The speech flagged in interest for a consider.
able period after this, and a prosess of "thin-
ning" began in the galleries and at the sides of
the area. Mr. Disraeli, however, rewarded
those who listened to him closely, as the vast
bulk of
,the meeting undoubtedly did, by a
clever and telling attack upon the Premier
for the " uncertain sound" which he gave
out on great questions. Did Sir Charles
Dilke profess himself a Republican —the
Prime Minister of the Crown spoke of
hire. as
,a "fellow-labourer." Was it
proposed to abolish the House of Lords—the
Prime Minister said the subject was a difficult
one, and he would think twice or thrice before
he undertook it. Did Mr. Miall (an unani-
mous groan rent the air)—did Mr. Miall pro-
pose to disestablish the church—the Premier
suggested that it must be obvious that the
temper of the House was not at that moment
favourable to the' plan, and Mr. Miall should
"act upon opinion out of doors." Accordingly
Mr. Miall called meetings, and said, " I am
instructed to seek you to pass resolutions."
All these "told " immensely, and the
audience laughe'l and cheered with enthu-

cries of impatience, and on the left of the
speaker there was heard more than once or
twice, "What about the Alabama claims P."
That was precisely the subject, however,.
which it -aeon became obvious that Mr. Disraelt

He spoke feelingly of the condition of the
agricultural labourer, and urged with great force

" programme " of Conservative :policy came
not. During the last hour of the speech there
was audible a subdued murmur throughout
the hall, which spoke intelligibly, enough of
disappointment. A ringing cheer rewarded
Mr. Dieraeli's more than earnest vindication
of the late Earl of Mayo as a statesman and
the ruler of Ireland during a troubled period;
and there were symptoms of reviving in-
terest when the speaker, plainly gathering
himself up for a final eflort, referred to the
" unsatistaotory " state of our home and
foreign affairs. In the noxt breath, however,
he admitted • that the people were "pro..
sperous." The cheering was loud and hearty
when the ex-Premier sat down, but we *hell
not be wrong In saying that, as a political
manifesto which was expected to have a great
effect in stimulating the "Conservative re-
action," the speech was an admitted failure.

LONDON SCHOOL BOARD.

ELECTION FOR WESTMINSTER

FELLOW RATEPATERS.—I have been invited again to
offer myself as a candidate for a seat at the London School
Board now vacant in the Westminster Division.
The Education Act has not been a success. It has led
to theological and denominational discussions, rather than
to united and intelligent efforts on behalf of National
Education. This has convinced me that all causes of dis-
sension should, as far as possible, be removed; and as
what is called the religious difffoulty, is the main obstacle
in the way of practical educational work, I consider that
in any system of National Education, the State should
make provision solely for the secular instruction which
all children may receive in common; and that the respon-
sibility of the religious teaching of the young should be
thrown upon the various religious bodies.
The Act was passed to provide a good and useful secular
education for every boy and girl in England. No school
was to receive a farthing of public money unless conducted
on principles entirely unsectarian. The sending of child-
ren within certain ages to school was to be, by degrees at
least, compulsory; and, to this end, the schooling was to
be gratuitous in the case of those whose parents were
without means of paying for it.

llad the Act been carried out in this spirit by the Lon-
don School Board, the education of the children of working
men would not have been delayed, and the bitterness of
feeling now existing among religious parties would have
been narrowed,

As the question of the payment of Denominational Fees
is yet undecided by the Board, it is important for those
who are against this system to avail themselves of the
Present vacancy, and secure the return of a candidate who
is against it.

It is agT cod that, in a question concerning the interest
of the people, they should be represented by some men
from among themselves, and I, therefore, offer myself in a
district to which, by long residence, I belong, and for
which there is reason to believe that I should have been
elected in November, 1870, had proper arrangements been
uytde for taking the votes.
Relying on your support for ultimate success,
I am, yours obediently,

GEORGE POTTER.

COMBINED AND CO•OPERATIVE

THE holiday week has been a time of con-

different parts of the country. While the
persuadeable youth of South Lancashire were

THOMAS ILuxrDA.Y in the chair. To this

Forest of Dean, North and South Wales, and
the neighbourhood of Bristol. For the
" Momentous " proceedings, as the PRESIDENT

ciation was considerably extended by the

flax-spinners of Leeds have endeavoured to
divide the working hands by offering a slight

accept no compromise. At two mills only
have the hands given way, while the iron-

articles.title: GREAT AND GOOD MAN GONE.
articles.text:
A GREAT AND GOOD MAN GONE.

THOUGH FREDERICK DENISON MA.VRICE
was an old man, his decease has taken the
public by surprise. Hd was in many respects
a great, and in all respects a good man. As
the original founder and the faithful promoter
of the Working Men's College, ho claims a
tribute of gratitude and admiration from all
connected with that section of the national
community. If, as a moral and philosophical
teacher, he was sometimes obscure and mys-
tical, it was impossible to avoid the catching
influence of his generous impulses; and at
least the broad principles of his philo-
sophy appealed successfully to ordinary
apprehensions. His religious views were not
always easy to understand. Born and bred
a Dissenter, and unable to take a degree in
Cambridge because unable to subscribe to
Church of England standards of faith and
practice, he proposed to himsolf to join the
Bar 1; but, being of a very serious turn, he
carefully reviewed his conclusions on the sub-
ject of religion, and, assisted, probably, by the
two brothers HARE, both Churchmen, recon-
ciled it to his conscience to seek holy orders,
preparatory to which he entered and graduated
at Oxford. We had ourselves watched his
career for more than forty years, and had
come to this persuasion, that he acquired a
belief in the eternal salvation through CHRIST
of the whole human race, and never abandoned
the hope of convincing Christians of all de-
nominations that it is their common duty and
privilege to unite in this pleasant creed.
1177MAuiticE's earliest companion of note
was JOIN STERLING, son of Mr. STERLING of the
Times. The two young men were at Cambridge
together, and both, contrary to first expect-
tation and tendency, became clergymen. They
were more ardent in the study of the modern
German literature than in attendance upon
college lectures and pursuit of the Univer-
sity course. Mr. MAURICE openly avowed to
a young man who consulted him about going
up to Cambridge, that he regarded the learned
society of the place, the seclusion of collegiate
life, and the free access to books, as the main
advantages of keeping terms. It is a curious
proof of the effect of such views, that, in a
school of learning to which he was not in-
debted for even a degree, ho should have been
called, in after life, to fill the Chair of Moral
Philosophy.
It has been stated that JOHN TERLING
owed more to his association with MAURICE
than to his converse with any other
man except COLERIDGE. The character
and disposition of his oollego friend
were such, so pure and so mild,
that no susceptible mind could fail to be
benefited by contact with them. With re-
spect to principles and views, however, the
results of such companionship were loss cer-
tain. The perceptions of STERLING were
quick, his curiosity was eager, and his appre-
hensions were prompt; but, with MAURICE,
all ideas of the abstruse were matters of much
obscurity and mystery, if not of some doubt.
Even COLERIDGE, who, though cloudy, could
be definite and oceasionally precise, did not
succeed in making all things either in heaven
or on earth perfectly clear and restfully con-
clusive te his attached pupil's mind. GOETIIE
and other Germans surpassed him in point of
telling influence, and it required all the
argument, learning, and eloquence of his best
friend and master, Archdeacon hun, to guide
him into the quiet harbour in which he
dropped anchor at last. The present Bishop
of Sr, DA,yrD'B is the only one left of that
immediate sehool of ecclesiastical thinkers,
though the Broad Church in general may be
considered as, more or less, their scientific
progeny.

Kivu= and &mum entered public life
together. With CHLRLES BULLER and some
others they became attached to LUIES SILK
Buexixamtia whoa ho started a weekly news-
paper (the Sphynx) on Radical principles.
In that journal, and also in the Atheneum,
of which the eminent traveller was
likewise founder, they first exercised their
talents in the writing of leading articles,
art critiques, essays, tales, and reviews. But
there was a marked difference between them.
Bnatuice, who wrote a strong clear hand, had
great faoility in composition, and so mush as

a verbal alteration Was of rare occurrence in
his manuscript. MAursgE, on the contrary,
was slow, confused, unable to satisfy himself,
always labouring, often in vain, to work out a
clear meaning, sending up to the printer at
the last moment, copy blurred, blotted, and
interlined in every direction; and though,
when the proof came down, it was returned
almost as full of alterations as the manuscript,
the drift of the article after allwas frequently far
from being either perspicuous or certain. Nor
can there be a doubt in any mind accustomed
to clear thought and plain expression, that to
the end Mr. MAURICE, with all his moral
excellence and intellectual depth, was still
labouring after a fulness and lucidity of
evidence which he could neither attain for
himself, nor set before his readers.

articles.title: WARWICKSHIRE LABOURERS' UNION.
articles.text:
THE WARWICKSHIRE LABOURERS'
UNION.

THE dawn of the day of emancipation of the
rustic) serfs from the not always mild despotism
of landlords and farmers is palpably streaking
the horizon with rays of hope. It seemed as if
the first shaft of rosy red showed itself over
the fields of South Warwickshire ; but we find
that tho Aurora has already become visible in
Herefordshire and had spread the light of pro-
mise towards parts of Gloucestershire, Salop,
and Wilts. Nevertheless, the fashionable
town of Leamington was destined to witness
the formation and announcement of an
Agricultural Labourers' Union, which, if pre-
ceded by a similar organisation in the cyder
districts, will probably more immediately and
more widely lead to corresponding associations
of the field labourers in all parts of the
kingdom.
The Warwickshire labourers have been
fortunate in the kindly encouragement and
good counsel that have come to thorn from
several quarters. There has appeared among
them a special commissioner from the office of
the Daily News, who evidently has a heart to
feel for them in their woos, and is taking care
that their hard case and patient conduct shall
he made fully known to the general public. The
Honourable AUDERON lIEnnEnT has espoused
their cause with a, temperate heartiness the value
of which is doubled by the circumstance of its
coming from the brother of an Earl. Mr.
EDWARD JENKINS, the Barrister, was found at
the side of the Member for Nottingham. Lord
EDMUND FITZMAURICE, Mr. MUNDELLI, Mr.
THOMAS HUGHES, Mr. GEORGE DIXON, Mr.
ANDREW JOHNSTONE, and Mr. A. H. BROWN,
unable to be present, joined in a letter full of
sympathy and wise suggestion.
It is but due, however, to the men them-
selves to acknowledge that, in spite of their
unfamiliarity with modes and measures of
organisation, they contain within themselves
individuals quite equal to the emergency
which has arisen. The practised trades
unionists of neighbouring towns came
promptly to their help, and, no doubt, both
aided them from their own experience, and
heartened them by their exhortations. With
true sagacity, however, the untrained rustics
resolved to stand or fall by themselves, to
avoid the reproach of bringing the trades of
towns in hostile array against country em-
ployers, and, if possible, to convince the
owners and occupiers of land th at they com-
prehend their own interests, and arc prepared
to assert and vindicate them without ex-
traneous help.
Among a class of men so little given to
reading and reflection as the field labourers
are supposed to be, keenness of perception,
acuteness in reasoning, and power of speech
are qualities not looked for in much force or
abundance. It is forgotten, however, until
circumstances bring the real state of the ease
to light, that certain moral and mental influ-
ences have long been at work, even in the re-
motest villages of England. Had the clergy
of the Established Church and the resident
gentry chosen to deal with the understandings
and the hearts of the peasantry, they might
have moulded both to their will. But, to a
great extent, they have been content to leave
them in intellectual torpor, and to make their
only or chief appeal to that thankfulness for
the smallest occasional gift which' springs
from being kept down in an habitual condition
of penury preforablo to tlko workhotin only

for the personal freedom and family union in
which it leaves the fellow-sufferers. For the
last hundred years, nevertheless, a system of
religious instruction almost as complete terri-
torially as the State Church, and much more
efficient in reality, has been in operation.
'We refer to the " connexion " established
by JOHN WEsrx.v. Almost every consider-
able town from Berwick to Land's End,
and from Liverpool to Yarmouth, is
the head or centre of a "circuit," which,
within a radius varying from six to twelve
miles, embraces the outlying villages. In
each of these, there is a chapel or other
preaching place, together with a Sunday
school. Those chapels are regularly served,
occasionally, yet constantly, by the appointed
ministers, and statedly by a numerous band of
local preachers. The former are men of cul-
ture, the latter are laymen, engaged all the
week in trades and occupations. Among
these local preachers there are labourers as
well as farmers, and mechanics as well as
shopkeepers, merchants, and professional men.
Besides sermons and schools, there are class
leaders and classes, attended by every man
and woman received as " members of society."
Instead, therefore, of the Methodist farmers
and labourers being like the senseless clods of
the field, they are, in the first instance,
systematically taught, and, in the second in-
stance, become teachers in their turn. Thus
it has come to pass that these Warwickshire
labourers have found among themselves men
quite capable of leading them; men who
have the needful intellectual grasp and readi-
ness of speech, and, in equal strength, the
requisto faculty of moderation, restraint, and
control.

"Mr. Anon," for example, is described
by the special correspondent of the Daily
News, as "their apostle." If a meeting is
to be held, every one wants to know
whether he will be there. The moment his
"large bright eyes" are seen, every voice
cries, " GOD bless you, Mr. Anon " He has
to shake hands all round, and the women melt
into tears as they greet him. Ho has "a
balanced mind and a glowing tongue." When
he opens his lips, every word is devoured. He
speaks, we are told, "quite pointedly and
slowly, with a command of diction and an ease
of demeanour that might command attention
in the House of Commons, warming to his
work with fervid eloquence, yet never
losing his moderation of tone," At one meet-
ing of a thousand persons, he "poured out on
them his fervour, stirred their dull intellects
with the force of his reasoning, and, before the
meeting was done, they were regenerated.
LEWIS could not write fast enough to take all
the names that were tendered." This, too,
was the man who took the chair at the large
committee which organised the union, and,
in the presence of such observers as Mr.
AUBERON HERBERT, Mr. JENKINS, and Dr.
SANDWITTI, evinced his perfect fitness for the
occasion. "In the chair," says the correspon-
dent, " beseeming it well, simple agricultural
labourer as he is, sits Mr. Anon, maintaining
his position with a modest, manly dignity,
which shed a lustre on the order to which he
belongs." When an "organising secretary"
was wanted, this was the man "unanimously
appointed." In short, he is " the true head of
the agricultural labourers in this movement."
At the first rising, the dissatisfied men came
to him and asked if he would speak should
they call a meeting. Ho assented; and, from
that beginning, the upstir has grown to its
present dimensions, till we see five thousand
men and women marching to Leamington,
calling aloud for "Anon," and forcing them-
selves into the Union of which he is chosen
organising secretary.

As energetic as ho is eloquent, he is the
man for the occasion, "Full," we are told,
"of earnest fervour, and glowing with un-
tutored eloquence that stirs the pulses and
moistens the eye, be is on the tramp from
village to village, fulfilling now, as he reckons,
a mission, the vision of which has been steadily
before his eyes for the past twenty years. It
was good to hoar the calm resonance of his
voice. Ho held the people in willing chains;
he swayed them as if they had been wax.
Ho took the autobiographical strain at some
length, and putting his poluts with great

clearness and force, related how indignantly
he had met and repelled the suggestions of
candidates who had waited upon him during
an election. They were fighting, he declared,
for the recognition of the fact, that there was
no compliment as between employer and
employed, if the latter gave honest labour
for a fair reward, and that the idea of a com-
pliment or patronage was degrading equally
to the man who gave and him who took.
He referred to one employer who introduced
labourers from Oxfordshire, and, in one
instance, made a father turn out his son to
make room for a new corner, The pathetic
tremour and manly ring of his voice, drew a
thrilling response. 'Men, I'll tell you what
I had to do. My master said to me "Eighteen-
pence a day is all I shall give you." I had a
wife and two children; and I know my duty
to them before GOD, because of the vow I had
made to her at the altar, to be, to do, or to
die to keep them. I knew that would not
keep them, and I struck. I got into bad
report; nevertheless, I did it, and, in con-
sequence, had to put on my clothes on Monday
morning, and never took them off again till
Saturday night. I went away to work where
I could get higher wages. Sometimes I could
got nothing but straw to lie on. Once I slept
for nights on corded wood; but, ray friends, I
did it for this reason ; I thought if anyone was
to suffer, it was not my wife and children, but
myself; and ever since I've had the same
opinion, and now join with you to maintrin
that principle.' Then, amidst loud enthu-
siasm, ho mentioned that a lady at Wells-
bourne—Miss Rylands—had, on receiving
notice from the men, sent for a gentleman
from Birmingham to arbitrate, and had, on
his award, increased the wages of her people."
Who, then, is this Anon ? "In Bradford,"
answers the correspondent, "there dwells a
man who is at once a day labourer and a
Methodist preacher; a man far superior in
every respect to his class; not greatly enlight-
ened by culture, but with a keen, restless,
inquiring mind, a boldness of thought, an
independence of character, a reputation com-
manding wide respect, and a rough, fervent,
natural eloquence, that marked him out as
specially fitted by nature for galvanising into
vigorous action a movement that seemed half
frightened to assert itself, yet for which the
time was ripe." Nor is this the only man
whose namo and description give reason for•
believing that this waking up of the Warwick-
shire labourers to a sense of their rights is
traceable to the preparation unoonsoiously
given, and as unconciously received. under the
form of Methodist religious teaching. When
the question of entrance money and weekly
subscription came up, and the committee were
debating whether the former should be six-
pence or a shilling, and the latter twopence or
threepence, the smaller amounts were adopted
on the showing of " a labourer, who was also
a Methodist preacher, arguing with great
shrewdness that it was out of the power of the
labourers to pay the larger amount, and that
what was wanted was combination rather than
contributions." Although the epithet of
" Methodist " is not applied to other indivi-
duals, yet, from these examples, and from other
circumstances, it is highly probable that persons
of this description are numerous both among
the leaders, and in the rank and file. GEORCIE
PERT, who brought up the people of Moreton
to the meeting place under the great beech
tree; WILLUM NASIT, who summoned those
of Locksley ; "Old NED," who "hobbled
away to Walton " ; and JOIN LEWIS, " the
man of energy and go," who went round as
as bell-man and crier—all, as they are made to
pass before us, wear the stamp of staunch
Methodists. ARCH, we are told, is a teetotaller;
and though, on arriving, after a long search
through mud and. mire, at Leamington, those
who had the means indulged in morsels of
bread and cheese, washed down with half a
pint of thin beer, "the quiet docility of
the men was something beautiful. Not a
drunken man, not a riotous company, was to
be seen. The men seemed to have the con-
sciousness that they were to achieve their
position as rational beings, capable of self-
restraint, and. concentrated. on the assertion
of their right to ho free-horn British men, and -
not serfs."

The justness of this movement cannot be
questioned by any one who gives attention to
the facts. At present wages the men and
their families cannot 1)e maintained. The
farmers know that the work wanted cannot be
done by boys and youths. They must, there-
fore, pay wages that will support a family.
Union is the only way by which this can be
urged effectually upon them. It is unwise to
retort by crying out against "strikes."
Trades' unions prevent strikes, and the same
will be seen as the effect of this agricultural
union. Already some real relief has come. In
Herefordshire, the word is "emigration and
migration." Surplus hands have been sent
into Yorkshire, Lancashire, and Staffordshire,
where they get sixteen, or even seventeen
shillings, with cheap fuel, and others have been
helped across the Atlantic. Mr. Ault is daily
receiving offers of work at increased rates for
the Warwickshire labourers. Among others,
the authorities of the North Eastern Railway
want porters and timekeepers at from a pound
to twenty-three shillings a week. The land-
lords, the clergy, and the farmers tell them
that they are " protected " at home ; but
Ltrer StatrK INS replies, "If we be protected,
we be starved." How true this is, let the
correspondent declare.—" Yesterday I looked
in upon 4 family
,whieli might be taken as
typical, and to-day I have constituted myself
a day boarder. Rising early, in time for
breakfast, I made the eighth at the little
table on the flagged floor. Our breakfast was
dry broad, and a fluid in which a lively
imagination might recognise a distant flavour
ef tea. The wife owned to having put but
one spoonful in for the seven, and she was not
allowed to amend the record on behalf of tile
eighth. After breakfast she and I formed a
committee of ways and means. I was not
able to elucidate a surplus. I tried all ways,
and had to give it up in blank bewilderment.
There could be no doubt that the man's
wages, when his cottage was paid for, were
but 125., and that the only addition was the
3s, earned by the eldest boy. And hero wes
the home before me—the wife, meek, neat, and
trim; the children poorly clad, but neither
barefoot norm n rags; and only, as I made a
point of personally ascertaining, a few shil-
lings of debt. I may be a bad financier, and
therefore I give the reader the opportunity of
figuring out the problem for himself :
Wages Father's, 12s. ;

Leaves for butoher's meat, tea, sugar,
soap, lights, pepper and salt,
clothes for seven persons, boots and

shoes for seven persons, beer, inedi-

eine, and r, Qoket money, per. week £0 4 4.
Somotitnes the family dine off a. salt herring
and potatoes,; the herring divided into seven
portions. Often the only fare is dry bread ;
sometimes it consists of 'tea-kettle broth '—
a cometion of hot water with a few greens
and herb!), and a 'tag end' or two of bacon.
Potatoes cost 4s. ad. per eight gallons, so we
could not afford to be heavy eaters. In a
military prison the dinner diet used to consist
of three pounds of potatoes and half a pint of
milk per man. We had no milk, and, among
the eight of us, were certainly not the rations
of a couple of prisoners. I have not yet
dined an hour, and I fool as hollow as a drum ;
but I resist any fleshpots that may be acces-
sible, and turn my thoughts longingly towards
supper, which is to consist of bread and boiled
potatoes, without the fragments of bacon rind,
whieh the children devoured at dinner
time. What kind of a day's work
can You, expeet from a man fed like
this ?—and our to-day's fare is an average
of this famity's diet throughout the year."

The "East Essex Farmer" does not meet
this case. When be points out that in this
county some families earn as much as 255. to
355. a week, he says enough to make a War-
wickshire man's mouth water, but not enough
to make them content with their different lot,
especially when he adds that, if they are ob-

stinato now, they will repent of it in the
winter. It is much the same as to Canon
GIRDLESTONE, who advises those who have the
chance gratefully to accept 15s. a'week, at the
same time reminding them that the North
Devon labourer is only receiving 9s. a week.
The contrast, as Mr. IllweErr well observes,
between the wages received by labourers who
have never yet shown power to combine, and
the wages now offered to some of those who
have formed themselves into a union, will
probably be regarded. by the labourers gene-
rally as a striking illustration of the great
advantages to be derived from combinations.
The best advisers yet are those who tell them
that their first object should be to reduce the
supply of labour by migration or otherwise,
so as to prevent its exceeding the demand.
They will then be able to meet the employers
on. more equal terms. The employers, it must
always be recollected, have themselves set the
example of combining. Every farmers' meet-
ing is a sort of combination. Should you
obtain your present demands, it would no
doubt be advisable to devote a portion of your
increased earnings to the formation of a per-
manent society to watch over and protect your
interests. This would, at any rate, go far
towards preventing your being exposed to the
imputation that your increased earnings had
not benefited anybody permanently except
the publicans. Your society, when formed,
might usefully devote its attention to several
subjects with which, as well as with the rate
of wages, the interests of the agricultural
labourer are connected. Such subjects are,
for example, the extension of 'political rights
in the counties, the establishment of co-opera-
tive stores and savings banks, the extension
of the allotment system, the abolition of pay-
ments in kind, the present system of inclosure,
and those laws and customs which interfere
with the cheap transfer of land, with cottage
building, and the investment of capital in the
soil, thereby narrowing the field of employ-
ment and lowering the rate of wages. One of
the Most effectual means of improving your
position will be the passing of a general
measure of compulsory education. You will
thereby avoid the possibility of the labour of
your children being used as a means of under-
selling your own, while the education will
command a higher rate of wages than the
uneducated workman, He will also be more
capable of choosing the best field for his
labour. We have been told that you propose
to settle your differences with your employers
by arbitration.. Without venturing to give
an opinion' on this particular ease—with the
circumstances of which you are naturally far
bettor acquainted than we can be—we may
observe that in general, arbitration has proved
a most effectual means of settling such dif-
ferences as those now existing in Warwick-
shire, and is therefore well worthy of your
consideration and also that of your employers.
In conclusion, we express the pleasure with
which we have seen that the objeots you aim
at are of a practical character, 4ml that you
have preserved a studied tone of moderation
in the present controversy.

articles.title: THIRD CENTURY OF DUTCH INDEPENDENCE.
articles.text:
THE THIRD CENTURY OF DUTCH
INDEPENDENCE.

TriE Hollanders on Monday celebrated the
third century of their national independence.
This event is identified with the capture of
Bridle by their brave forefathers in the year
1.572. Having been driven out of the Low
Lands by the Spanish Duke of ALvA, the
confederates equipped a fleet in England,
entered the harbour of Brion° near the mouth
of the river Maas, compelled the enemy to
surrender the port and place, and made of
them the first seat of the Dutch Republic.
The town is famous also as the birthplace of
those naval heroes, VAN Tneur and DE

The rejoicings were universal through the
kingdom. The Hague was busy with banners
and garlands, and was at night the scene Of
fireworks and illuminations. Rotterdam distin-
guished itself by the most remarkable display.
A. procession of five thousand persons formed
along the streets and the quays, In a long
series of open waggons, the public saw the
representatives of ancient times and of
modern condition. Here, were the aborigines
of the country, clothed in skins and armed

with rude primitive bows and arrows. There
at the learned and Witty, ERASMUS at his desk
with two fools in motley lying at his feet,
showing folly vanquished by learning. All the
trades were appropriately typified, each at
work with appropriate tools. The Dutch, who
know what they owe to industry, thrift, and
perseverance, highly appreciated the significant
display. The ICING and his Ministers made
their appearance at Brielle, which was the
centre of the national festivity. His MAJESTY
laid the first stone of a monument to per.
petuate the memory of the national deliver-
ance, and echoed in a brief but outspoken reply
the stirring advocacy by the finest orator in
Holland of universal freedom, civil, religious,
and commercial.

By the taking of Bridle the brave and in-
domitable D utch cast off the yoke of a civil and
an ecclesiastical tyranny which they were not
able to bear. Then and there as elsewhere
and since, the despot and the priest were allies
in oppression. No wonder, therefore, that
what remains of sacerdotalisin in Holland was
stirred up to spoil, if possible, the commemora-
tion of the national freedom. At Bois-lesDue,
the bust of WILLrAm the Silent, that astute
yet heroic, and politic yet patriotic Prince,
was pelted with mud by the hirelings of
Papistical priests. The fortifications of the
place, called Pa,penbril, are a standing pro-
test against French incursion for Popish
purposes. When Louis BONAPARTE was King of
Holland, under the Empire of the first
NAPOLEON, the church of St. John in this
town was taken from the Protestants, after
two centuries of possession, and given to the
Romanists, who are numerous, and, as
appears, not less arrogant and insolent. At
13roda, likewise, which, in 1567, Alba an-
nexed to the Crown of Spain, but which, after
many changes, was finally rescued from the
foreigner at the General Peace, the Roman
Catholics, confiding in their superior num-
bers, refused to let the carpenters build an
arch of triumph; which, however, was
finished by the soldiers.
It may be hoped that in other places where
the proportions between Protestant and Ca-
tholic arc reversed, or where, at least, those
elements are socially and civilly intermixed,
Romanists are not wanting who would be as
loth as Protestants themselves to renounce
Dutch independence, and return to the yoke of
Spanish subjugation. Unfortunately, how-
ever, the influence of the priesthood, though
prudently restrained under circumstances not
favourable to its putting forth, is ever ready
to take advantage of superior numbers or
special opportunities; and it is only 'among
adherentp whom education has made thought-
ful and kali-respecting, that it does not possess
the power Of dictation and the means of en-
forcing its dictates. In the struggle for inde-
pendence, the true Hollanders had to fight
against terrible odds; but in native homo-
geneousness and in the courage and fortitude
which the sense of brotherhood inspires,
Divine Providence had supplied the never-
failing sources of eventual success. The
Dutch, as a people, have been made in a
manner perfect through suffering, and, by
patient endurance and untiring energy, have
come off more than conquerors in every en-
counter with foreign foes and natural disad-
vantages. Ages since, they were the best
educated nation in Europe; and though the
bigot PHILIP of Ham, who procured the
assassination of WILLIAM, decreed the extir-
pation of heresy from among them, a decree
which, under the bloody ALVA, the inquisition
turned into a formal condemnation of them
all to death, though tens of thousands of them
took refuge in England, yet even the women
of Haarlem rose in arms against the tyrants,
and rushed into the thickest of the fight.

All the world are debtors to the Dutch.
Not merely did their self-sacrifice and tenacity
of purpose wear out the constancy of the
Spanish generals and exhaust the Spanish
treasury, but they sent forth a voice which
shook the thione of every absolute monarch.
By a solemn Act of Abjuration, the States-
General deposed PnrtiP, and, appealing to
the law of nature, declared that men were
not made to be the tools of princes, but
princes to be the protectors of men, who,
whenever they become oppressors, may be

lawfully shaken off. CROIEWELL failed ill Ws
design to make the Dutch and the English Re-
publics mutually helpful by an interchange
of councillors; but nothing can ever prevent
the glorious histories of the two States from
being to each sources of peculiar pride and of
reciprocal strength.

THE PEASANTRY OF LINCOLNSHIRE.

THE county of Lincoln is one of those
agricultural districts in which the labourers
seem bent upon an improvement of their
condition and circumstan.oes. Within a dr'
eumference of fifteen miles' radius around the
Minster, clubs have been formed in nearly
every village, in which some thousands have.
enrolled themselves. The movement is novt
nearly two months old. Meetings have been
'general, and the attendance -his been nume-
rous, having regard to the population of each
place. With one exception they were orderly,
peaceable, and business-like. The exceptiop
occurred at Horneastle, a horsy place not so
quiet as most others in the country. It was
" statute-day," the general hiring day, and
much beer had been drawn and drunk. An
individual obnoxious, for some reason net
stated to the generality, took refuge in the
hostelry of an inn, whose doors were forced
and windows broken. But the disturbance was
quelled by the police, and the ringleaders were
punished by the magistrates, the affair having
no visible connection with the work and wages
question. This remarkable movement seems
to have broken out like spontaneous combus-
tion and to have spread like wildfire. "More
money and less time" is the rallying cry. At
the meetings the plan was the Methodist one
of each man telling his own experience, and
startling even to themselves, were the revela-
tions made of oppression laid on and suffering
endured. As a general result, the upshot le
that dearness of provisions and high rents
(averaging, it appears, five pounds a year)
make it indispensable to ask for an increase
of three shillings, or fifteen a week, besides a
reduction in the working hours. Every man
was to ask his master in a civil and respectful
manner, as a favour, to grant the advance,
and, if refused, to give a notice to cease work
on the Ist of March. The farmers, to a man,
rejected the demand, but many offered an
advance, refusing to entertain the ques-
tion of time. The men were unanimous in

"sticking to the terms," and, on the
day appointed, came out in a body.
The country was in consternation. Farmers
galloped about in wild disorder as if each was
taken by surprise. The men were calm,
quiet, and confidant. Work was at a
standstill. The determination of the men "
seized the farmers. Their tactics were to
"smash the clubs." To effect this they re-
solved to do without labour for a month.
Lincolnshire farmers are wall-to-do. The
hired servants might feed the stock, and
horses stand ia the stable. They would work
themselves; they were not the men to die
in a fog." The month is nearly expired, and
hardly a farmer has broken the bond. But
what about the men? A few, very few, have
"gone in" at 16s. ed., and something "lii
kind," but the bulk stand firm to their terms,
but not idle. They moved off at the outset, '
and got work in the towns and on rail war-
Some have even gone to the manufacturing dis-,
triots, so that nine-tenths of the whole ere
employ at from 3s. to 48. per day. In the
meantime, important seasonable work is
stopped. Not only is spring corn not in, but a
great deal of land is not ready. The present is
perplexing; the future gloomy and uncertain.
Something must be done, and soon, or the
consequences will be serious. Land cannot be
shut up like a shop. If not assisted to grow_
corn, it will grow weeds. What are wanted
are able arbitrators to do even justice.

A fatal machinery aceid.ent is reported from
Cornwall. At the foundry of Messrs. Williams'
at Helston, preparations were being nwle fo,r
casting, and the fire was being got up throne
blasts of air driven by means of a water wheo.
Suddenly the wheel stopped, and a youth
named Lander was found to be caught in tile
machinery. His body WO almost torn to
Pieces. A quarter of the •eireurderence
large iron cogged wheel, weighing 4 cwt.,
broken by the pressure of the poor fellow's
body.

articles.title: FRIENDLY__AND_BITILDING
articles.text:
FRIENDLY__AND_BITILDING

SOCIETIES.

The Second Report of the Commissioners
appointed to inquire into the operation of the
Ads relating to Friendly Societies and Benefit
Building Societies has been issued, and it is
deserving of special attention, inasmuch as it
embodies the conclusions to which the Com-
missioners have come as the result of their
inquiry. They complain that they had not
sufficient powers to make their inquiry into
certain portions of the field committed to them
for investigation as exhaustive, as they desired,
and they suggest whether some further in-
quiry should not be carried out by authority
of Parliament. With the general question,
however, they deal fully, and the recommenda-
tions with which they conclude their report
are certainly worthy of serious consideration..
After pointing out the advantage of per-
manent as distinguished from terminable
building societies, the Commissioners refer
to the fact that the great development in the
operations of these societies has almost entirely
changed their character. They still retain
their original character as societies for assist-
ing members, on the mutual principle, to
build, but they have also become societies for
receiving and lending money, this privilege
being extended in some instances to none
members. This has no doubt introduced a new
element into building societies, and it is not
on entirely free from objection, because where
the powers of borrowing are unlimited, and the
powers of lending are not restricted to mem-
bers investing, as a condition of their becom-
ing borrowers, there is a tendency to rush
into speculation as a means of making profit.
The best of these sdcieties are those which
have not sought to make a profit, but have
been conducted on the principle of giving to
the borrower and lender equal advantages.
So far as we understand the recommendations
of the Commissioners, they appear to contem-
plate a society very much of the character of
the principal society in this part of York-
shire. _ _

They would still maintain these societies,
dropping the prefex "benefit," as distinct
from joint-stook companies, and continue
their registration with the Registrar of
Friendly Societies. They would also extend.
the privilege of paying small sums on nomina-
tion or on intestacy without letters of
administration to a maximum of £5O. On
the other hand, however' they would limit
the amount which should exempt from stamp
duty on mortgages to £2OO, abolish the
privilege of priority against the estates of
deceased debtors, and restrict the borrowing
powers to two-thirds of the total value of the
amounts for the time being secured on mort-
gage; or, as an alternative for terminating
societies, to six months' subscriptions. The
limit as to stamp duty is, we think, too low.
At the same time it is only fair that the law in
this respect should be altered, as these so-
cieties have been used very extensively by
borrowers other than those for whom they
were intended, The limit as to borrowing
powers is that fixed in some of our best
societies, and, we would rather see it lowered
than raised. A large loan fund has its dan-
gers as well as its advantages. These societies
have done an immense good to all classes, and
all that.it is desirable to do in legislating for
them is to keep them as far as the law can
keep them within the limits of safety. The
public has confidenee in them, not because
they yield large profits, but because they are
believed to afford a safe investment for small
periodical savings. „.

articles.text:
WEST-END LONDON BOOT CLOSERS'
SOCIETY AND THE 'EXHIBITION?

On March ,25th a meeting of the members
and friends of the Boot Closers' Society took
place at the Golden Lion, Mr. Darlington's,
Wardour-street, Soho, on the occasion of the
presentation of the medals awarded by the
Council of the international Workmen's
Exhibition of 1870 to the members of the
West-End Boot Closers' Society. Mr.
Thomas Warren, senior, presided.
The Chairman congratulated the members
for the excellent manner in which the exhibi-
tion had been conducted, and thanked the
committee for their unpaid services in render-
ing the affair a success, and the members
who so generously came forward to assist the
trade and committee in the produotion of
work
.deserved their warmest support, e.nd
fully justified the position of the West-
End Closers as workmen that could not be
excelled for workmanship or beauty of design.
Thefl large number of medals brought off by
the trade was the best proof of his assertion.
Mr. John Dickinson pointed out to the trade
the difference of the Exhibitions of 1861,
1862, and 1870. In the two former exhibitions
the employers were acknowledged, and. not
the real workman; in the latter the workman
was allowed to represent himself, and honour
was given where honour was due.
Mr. Charles Murray, in the name of the
trade, thanked those members who so kindly
came forward to assist the committee, and
made the display of work worthy of the West
Riad Boot Closors' Society, Lie stated that

he had only returned to England within the
last few weeks, after an absence of fifteen
months in the United States, and he could
assure them after having travelled some fifteen
hundred miles west of New York, that in no
town or city did he find any work that
could be compared to the work of the West-
end, although in many cases the rate of wages
was nearly double to what it was in London.
On the whole the trade must feel highly
gratified with the awards obtained at the
Workmen's International Exhibition.

Mr. Browning, one of jury of the Inter-
national Exhibition, stated that he accepted
the responsibilities with a determination on his
part to see justice done to all parties, and he
would mention what was not known to many,
that the council had only allowed one gold
medal for the whole of that class of work,
which included all leather work. He (Mr.
Browning) at once saw that such an arrange-
ment would be most unfair to many ex-
hibitors, and especially to the West-End
Closers' Society, and in a report which he
drew up to the council he pointed this out
to them, and it had the effect of their altering
their decision, and awarding the Closers'
Society two gold medals, and similar awards
to others, instead of one gold medal on the
whole class.

The Chairman then. presented to Messrs.
John Edwards and Richard Sling° a gold
medal; to Messrs. Waller, Shepherd, and
Samuel Bavystock, a silver medal; and to
Messrs. John Dickenson Francis, Peter Saun-
ders, Frederick Burt, William Colebrook, and
Henry Cobbold, a bronze medal.

articles.title: LONDON NATIONAL 'SOCIETY FOR WOMEN'S SUFFRAGE
articles.text:
LONDON NATIONAL 'SOCIETY FOR
WOMEN'S SUFFRAGE

On the 26th instant, Miss Reedy, M.A..,
read a paper on Women's Suffrage at the
Assembly Rooms, in IChenies-street, Totten-
ham Court-road. The:Rey. Edwin A. Abbott,
Head Master of the City of London School,
took the chair. In introducing Miss Beady,
Mr. Abbott said that if he considered the
claim of women to the suffrage merely as a
matter of abstract right, he should not think
it worth while to come forward publicly in
support of it; but, looking at the matter from
a practical point of view, he had come to the
conclusion that the removal of the electoral
disabilities of women would have an important
effect in remedying an existing evil. He
then dwelt on the educational disadvantages
under which women now labour, the want of
thoroughness in the instruction of girls under
the present system of private governesses, the
difficulty of obtaining endowments for girls'
schools and the frequency with which, in
oases of endowments originally intended for
boys and girls, the girls had gone to the wall;
and said that he could not help thinking that
if even a small number of women were once
upon the electoral roll, Members of Parliament
would lend a much more ready ear to the
appeal for better educational arrangements
for girls than they were now disposed to do.
Mr. Abbott ended by saying that he could not
see how giving a vote to a woman should
make her unwomanly. For his part, he
believed that it could only tend to the en-
nobling of her character that she should take
a real, true, and responsible interest in political
questions.
Miss Beady, in her lecture showed that the
political enfranchisement of woman would
have a wholesome moral effect on the corn-
munity by placing women, who are the natural
instructors of youth, in a position of fuller
moral and intellectual responsibility, and thus
necessitating for them a higher education than
they at present receive, She disclaimed all
intention of placing women in opposition to
men, or of setting them up as superior to men.
She was inclined to agree with Mrs. Poyser,
that "women were foolish enough—God hail
made them to match the men." Neither did
she think that there was any ground for fear-
ing that as soon as opportunities of political
and professional activity were open to women,
they would despise domestic duties. She
could not understand why the routine of
domestic life should be loss attractive than
the office drudgery of men. If it seemed so
now, it was only because public opinion had
attached to the latter a dignity and credit it
denied to the former. Miss Beedy concluded
by moving a resolution in favour of Mr. Jacob
Bright's bill.
Mrs. Burbury, in seconding the resolution,
corroborated from her experience as a trustee
of the North London Collegiate School for girls
what the chairman had said about the diffi-
culty of getting endowments for girls' schools
and colleges.
Before the resolution was put to the meeting,
Captain Macse, speaking from the audience,
said that having a very groat general sym-
pathy with this movement, he had often
regretted that he could not give it his chief
being
aor.t, But it seemed to him that women
vertical and not a horizontal section
of society, it would be a mistake to enfran-
chise the top layer—the women with property,
at a time when the propertied classes were
already disproportionately represented.. Why
not ask for the suffrage for all women?
Mrs. Maelaren, also speaking from the

audience, reminded Captain liaixse that among
the working classes there were a large number
of single women and widows earning their
living and paying rates, and added that as a
matter of expediency it was better not to aS4,-
too much.

The resolution was carried unanimously.
Mr. Warr, in proposing that a petition in
favour of Mr. Jacob Bright's bill should be
signed by the chairman for the meeting, said
that we must either grant the suffrage to
women, beginning with some few who would
at any rate represent their sisters better than
any class of men could do it, or fall back on
vicarious representation. Working men had
been told before the Reform Bill how great
were the advantages of vicarious representa-
tion; but they had not been content with it,
and had agitated till they had got direct
representation. That vicarious representatioa
did not work quite satisfactorily for women
was shown by the injustice of the existing
marriage law, of which Sir Henry Maine had
said that it was the most barbarous law exist-
ing in any civilized society.
Miss Morgan, M.D., in seconding the reso-
lution, said that it was undeniable that
women suffer practical disadvantages for
want of the suffrage; for instance, it was no
unusual thing for women to be refused as
tenants, because, if they wore accepted, the
vote would be lost. ,

The resolution was carried unanimously,
and the proceedings terminated with votes of
thanks to tho lecturer and the chairman.

articles.title: TUNNEL UNDER THE MERSEY.
articles.text:
THE TUNNEL UNDER THE MERSEY.

One of the grandest works of modern times
affecting this locality has now been com-
menced, in the construction of the tunnel
which i to conned Birkenhead and Liverpool,
and to give the much needed communication
between the two branches of the great dook
estate on both sides of the river. The result
of this great work must be most beneficial to
all—to the commerce of Birkenhead as well as
that of Liverpool, and to the town itself, apart
from its conneotipn with the docks. The trade in
the docks has 'been very much retarded for the
last few years, and. pro vented from ever attaining
its proper dimwww, by the want of sufficient
means for the transit orgoeds from Liverpool.
It is thought that the scheme of river ap-
proaches now being -carried out would sap&
that desideratum—but a moment's reflection
will suffice to show that even could carts and
waggons be able to cross the river without dis-
charging their loads, the advantage this
gained would be but a drop in the bucket of
the requirements of a vast system of steam
docks like Birkenhead, with the future before
them which every one who can see an inch
before his nose must be aware is certain to result
from the overspread of commerce to tho west
and best side of the Mersey. The scheme is
most magnificent one, and may indeed with
truth be termed a national work such as never
has been before attempted in this country. The
tunnel" will be about three miles in length,
about one-third of which will be under the bed
of the River Mersey, and will connect nearly
all the railways in England with the Birken-
head Docks. The effect of this gigantic
undertaking, as well as of the splendid river
approaches—a sister scheme, and working
in the same direction—cannot but be in the
highest degree beneficial both to our com-
merce and our local trade. The improvement
has already commenced. Never since 1805
has there been such a demand for house pro-
perty, and it needs but little prevision to see
that after
_waiting so long our tradesmen will
have a busy time of it ere long. The preli-
minary operations for the formation of the
tunnel have been completed. A hording has
been erected on the south reserve land between
Shore-road and the river, close to Woodside
Ferry, and on Monday a number of workmen
commenced preliminary operations for sinking
a shaft in order to obtain the depth of 70 feet
below the bed of the river, at which point the
cutting of the tunnel railway will be under-
taken. The contractor for the work is Mr.
Johnson Dickson, of Whitby, Yorkshire, and
the engineer, Mr. Mackenzie, whose offices
' have been established in Bridge-street. The
tunnelling will be performed with two
machines, each of whieli will make a cutting
15 feet in diameter with a pressure of 30 horse
power engines. We understand that two
other shafts will be sunk on the Birkenhead
aide, one on the upper aide of Shore-road and
the other between the gas-works and Green-
lane, Trimmer°, where will be situated what
may be called the Cheshire terminus, the line
there joining the Birkenhead and Chester
Railway, thus giving direct access from
London into Liverpool, under the Mersey. As
most of the materials dislodged in the cutting
will be brought to bank at Birkenhead, it will
be some time before the work commences on
the Liverpool side the only debris tobe brought
up there being that displaced in the down-
ward shaft, which will have to be driven in
order to reach the eastern end of the tunnel.
This will be near the harbour-master's office.
It is anticipated that unless serious geological
oi faults " are met with, the outting of the
tunnel, which is to aecommodate double line
of rails, will be completed, in two years. We

need not any we wish the project well. It will
prove One of the greatest arteries of railway
communication in this district, and must
eventuate greatly to the advantage of the town
in every respect.

articles.title: YOUTHFUL HEROISM REWARDED.
articles.text:
YOUTHFUL HEROISM REWARDED.

A remarkable instance of oourage in a more
child has just been rewarded by the Royal
Humane Society by the presentation of its
silver medallion, together with handsome
testimonials, to a little boy named Charles A.
Smith, only nine years of 4.e, the son of a
gentleman in the Civil Service, for rescuing
his little brother, who had accidentally fallen
into the River Yarra, from drowning at Mel-
bourne, Vietoria, in December last. It appears
that the attention of the mother of the child
was suddenly attracted by ()ries of alarm from
the opposite side of the river raised by. a gen-
tleman who witnessed the child fall into the
water; and upon running,. down the garden
to the margin of the stream she discovered to
her horror that her youngest child, some 18
months old, whom she had sent out in charge of
a nurse, had fallen into the water, and
was drifting rapidly away with the strong
current that was running, little more than a,
tiny arm being visible above the surface. An
elder boy, who was just learning to swim, had
fortunately also beard the alarm' and acorn-
paned his mother. Seeing the danger of the
baby, without a minute's hesitation, this
plucky little fellow hastily threw aside some
of his clothes and sprang in boldly to the
assistance of the drowning ohild. Reaehing
him with considerable difficulty, he managed
by dint of desperate paddling and struggling,
to keep himself and his little burden afloat
until a semi-submerged snag caught and
providentially arrested their progress. Here -
he held on for some time, and was rapidly
becoming exhanstod, and shouted that he
could hold on no longer, when an inward turn
of the current having swept them somewhat
nearer the bank, the mother was enabled by
wading in herself waist deep to catch the
brave boy by the hand, and draw him and the
other little one into safety. "
