articles.title: WEEK'S NEWS.
articles.text:
THE WEEK'S NEWS.

_Several severe shooks ,of earthquake were
felt on the 29th ult. in California, and con-
siderable damage was done in several small
towns.

The inhabitants of St. Ives, Hunts, have
resolved to recognise the success of Mr. J. H.
D. Goldio as stroke of the Light Blue crew by
a public dinner, to which Mr. Goidle is to be
invited, Officers have been appointed to bring
the project to a successful issue. The father
of Mr. Goldie is the vicar of St. lves.

The wholesale execution, without trial, of
the Koolcas, who lately revolted under a
fanatical impulse, and upwards of 60 of whom
were blown away from guns, has been con-
demned by the Indian authorities. The papers
on this subject will shortly be laid before Par-
liament.

The Mayor of Bolton announced on Mon-
day at the Borough Court that ho had received
a letter from the Home Secretary, to the effect
that he has directed inquiry to be made into
the occurrence of November last, when riots
arose after a lecture by Sir Charles Dilke, and
William Schofield was killed.

On Monday the Andalusian train arrived
late in Madrid owing to its having been
attacked the previous night near Manic Anares
(?) by brigands. The robbers took up the rails
and arrested the train which they plundered
with deliberation, taking £3,000 of the coth-
pany's money, and other booty. They wounded
throe persons who resisted.

The death of the Rev. Frederick Denison
Maurice is announced. The cause was pleurisy,
to which he rapidly succumbed, close upon his
70th year. Deceased was the son of a Uni-
tarian minister, but himself a minister of the
.Church of England, and a famous preacher.
He retired from King's College in consequence
of his views on eternal punishment. He was
elected Professor of Moral Philosophy at Cam-
bridge in October, 1866, and received the
honorary degree of M.A. in March of the
following year.

On the Ist inst. ,an excursion train from
Birmingham, on the Groat Western Railway,
left the metals near Acock's-green station, five
miles from Birmingham. Eighteen of the
twenty carriages forming the train followed.
Only a few of the passengers were slightly
Injured. One young woman iiad her nose
broken and teeth displaced, and one or two
others were slightly bruised. All the pas-
sengers, except the young woman, went on to
Stratford-on-Avon, when a fresh train arrived.
The cause of the accident is wholly inex-
plicable.

Mr. Alfred t3hoolbred, a son of the head of
the well-known firm in Tottenham-court-road,
died, very recently at hie residence, Surbiton-
park, on the 30th ult. The cause of his death
is supposed to have been heart disease. The
deceased gentleman was a prominent member
of the Oscillators Rowing Club, of which lie
was one of the founders. The event is greatly
deplored in the neighbourhood, where the
family have a very numerous circle of friends.
The deceased was out in the hunting-field, a
few days before his death.

On the 28th ult., the House of Win.
Hunter, a dairyman at Brunstane, near
Portobello, was found to be on fire, and two
of his children were burnt to death. It
appears that Hunter and his wife had gone to
Edinburgh on business, leaving the children
in bed, and that in their absence a burning
coal fal from the fire, and the flameseatended
to the furniture.

Dr. Deane, Q.C., has been appointed the
new Vicar General of Canterbury, in the place
of Sir Travers Twiss, resigned, by the Arch-
bishop, and Dr. Tristram, the Chancellor of
London, by. the Bishop of London. Sir
Travers I'?118S is unable at present to folio w
i his profession as a barrister n consequence of
severe illness.

The Controller of the Stationery Office is
able to show a material reduction in the con-
sumption of pens by the public departments.
In the finanoial year 1806-67 they used 14,433
gross of steel pens, which cost £3,836, and
860,267 quill pens, which cost £1,722. In
the year 1871-72 the consumption (partially
estimated at present), though larger than in
the preceding year, is but. 12,463 gross of
steel. pens, costing ,X 1,585 and only 478,761
quilt pens, costing

On Monday tho tramway communication
between Csanden-town and King's-oross was
opened for traffic). The linos between the
Easton-road, Kentish-town, the Brecknook,
and. Camden-town are now completed; and
should the Bill before Parliament, which pro-
poses that the lines be carried along Penton-
vine and King's-cross-road, be passed, the
line of tramway from the north-woo of London
will be carried to the City.

Last week the number of paupers in the
workhouses of the metropolis was 34,486, and
83,789 received out-door relief, making a total
of 118,275. Compared with the corresponding
week in the years 1871, 1870, and 1869, these
figures show a decrease of 24,096, 45,402, and
33,502 respectively. The whole number of
vagrants relieved was 786.

An order has been made by Mr. Registrar
Hazlitt for delivering to the Tichborne Claim-
ant his wearing apparel and papers at the
Waterloo Hotel. The former was said to be of'
little value, but the possession of the docu-
ments was alleged to be necessary for properly
conducting his defence.

On Wednesday the Grand Jury at the
Middlesex Sessions returned a true bill against
Earl Cadogan, on account of a nuisance which
had been permitted to exist upon some of his
lordship's property in Chelsea. The fences of
the Manor estate having been removed, the
place had become a rendezvous for indifferent
characters, and on Easter Monday the scene
of disorder was a cause of great annoyance to
the neighbourhood. Hence the action which
has'now been taken to prevent a repetition of
such proceedings.

Mr. W. A.. Redmond has issued his address
to the electors of Wexford. Mr. Redmond is
an advocate of home rule and denominational
education. He is in favour of reform of the
Irish grand jury laws; union rating, and a
general amnesty to the Irish political pri-
soners. Mr. Redmond is very popular in
Wexford.

A eorresp,ondent in Florence gives an account
of the unveiling there of the monument to
General Franti. The ceremony was carried
out under the direction of General Cialdini,
and a large number of other military men
were present, besides members of the Senate
and the Chamber of Deputies. Several
speeches were delivered in praise of the
gallant Italian soldier in whose honour the
monument has been erected, and a march
past of the troops concluded the proceedings.

It is believed that the East London Museum
will be opened before the end of the ensuing
month.

Communications from Odessa, published in
tho Moscow journals, mention the impression
produced on the masses by the theft of the
statue of the Virgin known as Kasperovskaiag.
It had been the object of a special veneration
on the part of
,the population, and was con-
sidered, so to say, the palladium of the town.
Several times a year it was carried in proces-
sion with great pomp in the neighbouring
looalities. The lower class persist in attribut-
ing the robbery to the Jews, without having
any ground whatever to confirm their suspi-
cion.

On. the 29 th ult. , the weaving faotory of Messrs.
Graham, Centre-street, Glasgow, took fire, A
five-storey building, the longest in South
Glasgow, one three-storey, and a weaving
factory, were all destroyed, nothing but the
bare walls remaining. Six girls, who had
stayed in the mills to take their dinners,
escaped with great difficulty, ladders having
to be raised to the windows of the fourth
storey, from one of whieh they were separately
rescued. The damage is covered by the in-
surances.

At a Cabinet Counoil held in Washington
on Tuesday, the reply of the English Govern-
ment to the American note on the Alabama
question was discussed. The New York
Tribune is of opinion, that the United States
Government cannot, without admitting care-
lessness, which should be followed by resigna-
tion, admit the indirect claims to be either
groundless or frivolous. Satisfaction is, ex-
pressed by the same paper at the prospect of
England submitting to the Geneva arbitration.•

The regular hunting season with the Royal
buokhounds terminated on Monday with a
meet on Maidenhead Thicket, the general
rendezvous, when there was a much greater
assemblage of the nobility and gentry in
carriages and other fashionable. vehicles than
has been witnessed for several seasons past,
and .it was noticed that the field was chiefly
eontined to the, well-mounted and regular
sportsmen from the immediate neighbourhood,
so well as a select muster of the celebrated
London division. Lord Cork (the noble
Master) was absent. The deer, on 'being
unearted, and after having a rather familiar
interview with the large number of pedestrians
who on this occasion assembled, went away in
gallant style in thedirection of Boyne-hill, the
rain falling in. torrents. Baton then turning
short to the left, went direct on to Marlow,
where he crossed the Thames into Buckingham-
shire, Although the Easter Monday's hunt is
considered to close the regular hunting season
of this Royal pack, there will be several bye
days, one of which will he in Windsor Forest,
for the purpose of giving the new whip, who
succeeded Harry Ring, an oppertunity of testing
the quality of the howls.

On Monday an accident, in which several
persons were injured, some seriously, occurred
at the laying of the foundation-stone of a
Wesleyan chapel, in the Prince of Wales-
road, near the Malden-road, Kentish-town.
Shortly after three o'clock a large number of
spectators bad assembled, and stands were
erected to accommodate them. One of these,
just inside the building, as the service was
proceeding, became too much crowded, and
gave way with a tremendous crash, the persons
who were standing on it falling a depth of
some ten or twelve feet on to rough rubbish
and brick, causing them serious injuries.

On Monday afternoon an inquest was held
at Albion-road, Stoke Newington, on the body
of George Blaber, aged 44, of the Cottage,
Milton-road, a retired florist who had com-
mitted suicide. No adequate reason could be
assigned for the rash aut, and the jury returned
a verdict of suicide whilst of Unsound Mind.

On Monday an alarming gunpowder explo-
sion took place at South Shields. A young
girl, fifteen years of age, named Jane Ellen
Gibson, daughter of a pitman living at
Temple Town, South Shields, while engaged
in lighting a fire took down a bottle of gun-
powder, mistaking it for train oil. She emptied
a quantity of it on the fire, the result being
that a terrific explosion immediately took
place. Part of the roof of the house was blown
off, and the walls were greatly shaken and
otherwise damaged. The girl was found to be
terribly burned, and now lies in a very
critical: condition.

Monday was a statutory Bank Holiday
under Sir John- Lubbock's Act of last year.
There was consequently an entire suspension
of business in the City, and throughout the
metropolis an increasing number of tradesmen
appeared to avail themselves of the opportunity
to close their shops. Unfortunately the broken
weather at once interfered with the enjoyment
of those who made their way towards the
outdoor recreations of the suburbs, and mate-
rially lessened the number of excursionists
from the home counties to London. The best
was, however, made by all of a very poor day.

An engineer named Sparkes was on Monday
convicted at Marlborough-street of having
struck one Henry Kelly upon the head with a
loaded stick, and was sentenced to six weeks'
imprisonment with hard labour, without the
option of a fine.

It is very probable that M. Thiers will at
once take up his residence for three weeks at
the Elys6e Palace. Preparations for his recep-
tion there have already been made. He intends,
however, to ask permission of the Permanent
Committee. The majority of the members are
believed to be opposed to the arrangement, on
the ground that if M. Thiers lives but for a
short time at the Elyse, Paris will be grati-
fied, and it may then be difficult to resist the
popular cry calling for the removal of the
Assembly to the capital.

The City Press says, it is stated that ere
long there will be a change of the judicial
ofncers of the Corporation, and that a vacancy
may occur both in the office of Recorder and
Common Serjeant.

The Junior Army and Navy Club are, it is
stated, about to leave their temporary quarters
in King-street, St. James's, and move to pre-
mises more suitable to the requirements of its
rapidly-increasing number of members.

On Good Friday, Benjamin Rose, employed
as sorewer at John Brown and Co.'s works,
at Sheffield, was on a raising platform regu-
lating a moveable crane, when one of the
handles struok him and caused him to fall
upon a red-hot armour plate which was being
rolled. lie was frightfully burnt, and died in
the hospital a short time afterwards.

The Messageries steamer Meandre, which
left on the 22nd ult. for Salonica, was found
to be on fire when between Gallipoli and the
Dardanelles. There were about a hundred
passengers on board, who were at once trans-
ferred and sent on to their destination' with
the mails and the money groups, on board
one of the Fraissenet Company's steamers.
The Meandre was then run ashore and sunk
at Galata-Bournou, this being found the only
means of getting the fire under.. Efforts are
now being made to refloat her, which it is be-
lieved will be speedily successful, The fire is
supposed to have arisen from some inflam-
mable material olandestinely shipped amongst
the cargo.

A Convention was signed on Wednesday
with the Portuguese .Government for the
establishment ofa cable between Lisbon and
the Brazils, by way of Madeira and Cape do
Verd,

Mr. Stansfeld addressed a crowded meeting
of his constituents at Halifax on Wednesday
evening. Tito right hon. gentleman defended
at some length the policy of the present
Cabinet.

An association has been formed in Spain for
the purpose of obtaining the restitution of
Gibraltar to that country.

It is announced from Madrid that the
elections throughout Spain have passed off
quietly, except at Cordova, where some slight
disturbances have occurred. The results thus
far, which include the returns from the prin-
cipal towns, show a considerable majority for
the Government. In Madrid, however, the
Opposition has gained the day.

A portrait of the late Mr. Sheriff Young was
on Wednesday formally presented to the AVie-
beach Town Council by the Speaker of the
House of Commons on behalf of a number o
subscribers. The right hon. gentleman con-
tested Cambridgeshire, in conjunction with Mr.
Young, at the last general election.

At Wednesday's meeting of the Commis
sioners of Sewers it was reported that within
the past fortnight 410811bs. of meat had been
seized in the markets and slaughterhouses of
the City as unfit for human food.

A Nonconformist Conference assembled at
Ipswich on Wednesday, when it was resolved
to endorse the declaration made at Manchester
in January last, that no candidate ought to
receive the support of Nonconformists at the
next election who would not pledge himself to
vote for the repeal of the 26th clause of the
Education Act.

A Correspondent of the Paris Temps, writing
from Madrid before the elections commenced,
says, that upon the resuli of those elections
the fate of the dynasty itself may perhaps de-
pend. Those who wish the existing Govern-
ment to remain in power, will vote for the
Ministerial candidates. Those who wish to
overthrow the existing Government will vote
for the candidates of the coalesced Opposition
Whatever may be the issue, everybody is
persuaded, the Correspondent of the Temps
says, that blood will be shed, and that the
Government, if defeated at the polls, will de-
fend itself by force of arms.

William Roebuck, a colliery engine-tenter
at Barnsley, has been committed on the
coroner's warrant for the manslaughter o
George Senior, a labourer employed in the
colliery whore Roebuck worked. It was
alleged that deceased was killed through the
negligence of Roebuck, who started the
ascending machinery before the proper signal
had been given.

Some misapprehension exists as to the
amount of the third class fare which the
Midland Railway Company are charging sine°
they commenced to carry third-class passen-
gers by all their trains. Their third-class
fares, though frequently lower than the par-
liamentary rate of a penny a mile, are never
in excess of that amount, and they have
not been increased in any instance since the
important concession which we announced
has been brought into operations We may
also add that the Midland Company ceased to
charge express fares to any class of passengers
many years ago, and charge ordinary fares by
all trains.

With regard to the prolifio nature of the
orange crops, more espeoially in an abundant
season, they are something really surprisingl,
Twenty thousand marketable oranges from
one tree seems almost beyond belief, bet, a
we have before stated, such is the fact; the,
branches have frequently to be propped up with
wooden supports to prevent, their breakinv.
Risso mentions a tree growing at Nice, In
1789, which was more than 50 feet high, and
the trunk of so large a, girth that it required
two men with outstretched arms to embrace it.
This tree usually bore from 5,000 to 0.004
oranges.

It is stated that for the first time withal
the memory of man, Lake Michigan has thi.
year been frozen over us far as the eye oaa
reach, the ice being from faux to eight inches
in thickness.

--
On Mr. Bushby taking his seat on the bench
at Clerkenwell Police-court on Tuesday, there
were but eight applicants for advice, and
thirty-three charges for hearing, Of thew
seven were for felony, and the remainder vier°
charges of drunkenness and assault. Th°
falling off in the number of charges is worthY
of remark. On Mr. D'Eyneourt taking ili3
seat at Marylebone, he had thirty-eight oharipo
to dispose of, being rather less than preYi"s
years.

At a meeting of the Leicester Town Coune)l,
it WIS unanimously resolved to petition both
Houses of Parliament in favour of the fill of
the Great Northern Railway Company for the
extension of their line front Newark to Leicos'
ter, and so bringing the latter town into direct
communication with Scotland and the north
and north-eastern portions of Eugland. 11114
giving easy access to the extensive agricultural
district of Lincolnshire and the coal fields of
South Yorkshire, whieli it is expected will be
of immense benefit to the town of Leicester.

Advices from Mexico announce that anarchy
reigns throughout Northern Mexico. The
revolutionists, after having been badly de-
feated, received reinforcements, resumed the
offensive, and have reooeupied Zacatecas.

Her Majesty Queen Victoria and the Royal
children daily make excursions to the various
objects of interest in the neighbourhood of
Baden. On the 29th ult. the Queen went to
nostril!, the Grand Duke having placed his
horses and attendants at the disposal of her
Majesty. The Queen has received no visitors
at her villa, with the exception of the Land-
grave of Hesse and the Duchess of Hamilton.

In the course of a lecture at Ryde the other
day, the Rev. Robert Moffatt, the African
missionary, referred to his son-in-law, Dr.
Livingstone, expressing his opinion that he
was quite safe, but was simply without re-
sources. His -impression was that he was
staying at the headquarters of some chief,
who, finding him friendly, and believing be
was a groat man, took charge of him, partly
under the impression that he would be well
paid when resources arrived for the traveller.
It was evident that Dr. Livingstone was un-
able to pay his way, and nobody could got on
under those circumstances. Ho (Mr. Moffatt)
had been 1,500 miles into the interior, and
knew the habits of the people as well as any
European living, and he felt positive that Dr.
Livingstone was still alive, for had he been
dead he was sure definite news would have
reached England long ago.

Advices from the Cape of Good Hope state
that the yield of diamonds is sensibly de-
creasing, and it is doubted whether any more
rich fields will be discovered. ,

On Monday, as an infantry officer was re-
turning to his barracks in Lyons, he was
attacked by several armed individuals, and
was forced to use his sword in self-defence.
One of his assailants was killed in the
souffle. The authorities of the city have com-
menced an investigation into the circumstances
of the affair.

A fire broke out at the Ladies' College, at
Baldoek, Hertfordshire, on Tuesday afternoon,
and the building was entirely destroyed. The
pupils and other inmates were rescued, but
were unable to save any articles, even of
wearing apparel. They were sheltered by
Mr. and Mrs. Edwards at the hotel. Happily,
no lives were lost.

A gentleman having been driven in a cab
from Stratford to Kennington-park, refused to
pay the fare, 78., and was summoned for it.
The cabman showed that as the hiring took
place outside the radius, he was entitled to
charge a shillinga mile for the whole distance.
i
The magistrate, n making the order for pay-
ment, thought it important that the public
should know of the existence of such a regu-
lation.

On Monday a large meeting was held at
Rotherham, the mayor in the chair, for con-
sidering the best means of obtaining puha-
` mentary representation for Rotherham. The
population of the proposed parliamentary
borough is 38,000. Resolutions were passed
that Rotherham should have representation as
it had greater claims than any other unen-
franchised town in the country, and than many
places having two members. A petition to
Parliament was adopted, praying for enfran-
chisement, and a dommittee was formed to
collect subscriptions to defray the expense of
obtaining the same. Rotherham is in the
centre of a large manufacturing district.

The contract for the new cable across the
Atlantic and direct to New York was signed
on Tuesday, and will be manufactured and
laid from the Great Eastern by the Teregraph
Construction and Maintenance Company, so
that the public is to be congratulated upon the
prospect of a fourth electric cable between
England•and America. It seems probable that
the 700 miles between Halifax and New York
will be laid first by another of the Telegraph
Construction and Maintenance Company's
fleet, and that the Great Eastern will subse-
quently lay the long lino between England
and America. The whole expedition will be
once more under Capt. Halpin.

According to the Oity Press a person named
Sarah Skelton, 104 years of ago, is in the re-
ceipt of relief from the City of London Union.
She was excused attendance recently, when
her allowance was renewed, in consequence of
the severity of the weather. She did not at-
tend, however, last Michaelmas at the union
offices. It, appears that she gained her settle-
ment in one of the City paribhes by living as
cook with Alderman Sir William Curtis, of
three •It's renown, who was sheriff in 1788, and
Lord Mayor in 1795.

It is announced that Lord Westbury has
accepted the post of arbitration on claims con-
nected with the European Assurance Society,
and that it is proposed to give him powers
Similar to those exercised by Lord Cairns in
the ease of the Albert Company.

On Monday, William Frederick Horry, a
young man of 28, underwent the extreme
penalty of the law at Lincoln, for the
murder of his wife, Jane Horry, at
Boston, on the liith of January last. On
Sunday afternoon the condemned man
received the Holy- Communion, and ap-
peared perfectly resigned. He went to bed at
ton o'elook, and rose at five thii next morning.
In conversation with the under sheriff, the
unfortunate man said that had the jury recom-
mended him to mercy they would have ex-
ceeded their duty. He walked very firmly to
the scaffold, and on the way fervently thanked
all the officials for their kindness. On the
scaffold he said—" Good-bye, Mr. Forster (the
governor). God bless you. God forgive my
poor dear father. God bless my poor children."
The bolt was then drawn, and death was
almost instantaneous.

Lord Lisgar, who is about to retire from
the office of Governor-General of Canada, was
better known as Sir John Young, and as having
held the successive posts of Chief Secretary
for Ireland, Lord High Commissioner of the
lonian Islands, and Governor of New South
Wales. He was raised to 'the peerage in
October, 1870. The Earl of Dufferiu, his
successor, is now Chancellor of the Duchy of
Lancaster, and received a promotion of two
steps in the peerage in November last. His
lordship is in his 46th year.

We rogret to announce that the Marquis of
Graham, son of the Duke of Montrose, died
on Wednesday evening in Mount-street,
Grosvenor-square. The Marquis returned
home from Homo about three weeks ago, and
shortly afterwards he was taken with enteric
fever. Sir W. Gull and Mr. Venning (of the
Ist Life Guards) attended him. The Duke of
Montrose Colonel and Lady Agnes Murray,
and Captain and Lady Violet Greville were
with the Marquis at his death. Thelate Marquis
of Graham was the second son of the Duke of
Montrose. He was born 22nd June, 1847,
entered the Ist Life Guards as cornet in July,
1866, and became lieutenant in August, 1867.

The Conservative banquet at Bath, at which
Col. Hogg and Lord Chelsea are to be present,
will take place next Thursday. The gathering
will be large and influential, and will include
the Duke of Beaufort, Mr. Richard Bright,
Mr. Gore Langton, Mr. Neville Grenville,
Lord Harry Thynne, Sir Geotge Jenkinson,
and other members of Parliament. The Bath
Chronicle says:—" Following, as it will, Mr.
Disraeli's magnificent reception in Lancashire,
it will show the strength of Conservative feel.
ing in this part of England not less effectively
than that reception has demonstrated the
same gratifying fact in the North."

In Dunkeld Cathedral a monument ltas been
erected to the memory of the officers and
private soldiers of the 42nd Regiment who fell
in war from the creation of the regiment to
the close of the Indian mutiny. The monu-
ment is by Mr. Steel, Edinburgh.

Snow fell heavily in the upper district of
Deeside on Saturday, and the showers con-
tinued on Sunday and Monday. A corres-
pondent of the Dundee Advertiser states the
depth on the lower ground at seven inches,
and says that the, accumulated snow on the
hills now measures several feet in depth.

Letters from the manufacturing districts of
France state that there is a general determina-
tion to petition the Government against the
duties on raw material. Arrangements are
also being made for holding meetings to pro-
test against the denunciation of both the Eng-
lish and Belgian treaties, and it is supposed
that this movement will spread all over the
country.

The cashier of the Bank of Ireland, in
Limerick, whose name is Fleury, has ab-
sconded, and it is supposed he has gone to
America with specie to the amount of £41,000.

A parliamentary return, obtained on the
motion of Mr. M'Laren, has just been issued,
which gives some statistics as to popula.
tion taxation, and representation. Ac-
cording to population, England should have
476 of the 658 members of the House of Com-
mons, Scotland 70, and Ireland 112. Accord—
ing to the sums paid towards the revenue,
England would have 514, Scotland 79, and
Ireland 65. At present England has 493
representatives, Scotland. 60, and Ireland
105.

The Kent Herald understands that the
Bishopric of Mauritius has been offered to the
Rev. Dr. Mitchinson, Head Master of the
King School, Canterbury, but he has declined
the post.

The Earl of Mayo, son of the late Govenor
General of tndia,,wjll attain his majority on
the 2nd of July next, in time to enable him to
take his seat in the Huns° of Lords in the
course of the present session of Parltament.
The noble earl is a lieutenant in the 10th
Hussars.

articles.text:
LATEST INTELLIGENCE.

FRIDAY.

A deputation of factory labourers waited
Upon Mr. Disraeli yesterday. Every impor-
tant town in Lancashire and every branch of
factory labour was represented. The deputa-
tion presented an address expressing their
approbation of the extension of the franchise
and their confidence in Mr. Disraeli's good
will towards their class and specially soli-
cited his attention to die nine hours move-
ment. Mr. Disraeli referred to the history
of the Ten Hours Bill, and the support which
he had given to that measure, and promised
his most careful attention to the subject.
M. niers will hold several receptions at the
Elysee during the recess.
The question of the restoration of the 200
millions of francs paid by Paris to the Prus-
sians is still pending between the Government
and the Municipality.
The Rappel announces that Count Arnim
arrived in Paris yesterday.

The funeral of the late Professor Maurice
took place to-day at Highgate Cemetery, at a
little before 1 o'clock.

• On Wednesday afternoon the attention of
the neighbours in Brewery-lane, Lancaster,
was attracted by tha fact that Vie house of a
malster, named Nathan Faulkner, was closely
shut up. On looking through the window
they saw Faulkner's ausekeeper, a woman of
50, named Jane Mason, lying on the floor,
apparently dead, and on the house
broken open by the police, this was found. to
be the CO:30. There was blood discovered
under her head. Suspicion, of course, fell
upon Faulkner, who had been missing all day,
and. the police soon found him concealed in
the loft of the malt-kiln where he worked,
having climbed the flue. He resisted- the
police who took him into custody, and refused
to say anything about the matter. The body
of the deceased woman awaits an inquest.
A return has been issued (en the motion of
Mr. Akroyd) relative to convictions for
drunkenness in Great Britain and Ireland,
from July 1, 1870, to July 1, 1871. The
population of Groat Britain and Ireland is
given at 32,845,780. The total convictions
wore 238,274, of which 23,175 were second
convictions, 12,065 were third convictions,
and 21.,84i more than three times. The total
number of summary convictions for criminal
offences of all kinds for the; same period was
637,887.

At the Kingston Assizes, yesterday morning,
before Lord Chief Justice Bovill, William
Chester Minor, 38, surgeon, was placed in the
dock on an indictment charging him with the
wilful murder of George Merritt. Strong
evidence having been given of the prisoner's
insanity, the jury expressed themselves satis-
fied, and returned a verdict of "Not Guilty,"
on the ground of insanity. The prisoner was
ordered to be detained during her Majesty's
pleasure.
It was reported at Lloyd's on Wednesday
that the Marian Ridley, from St. John's,
Newfoundland, for Barbadoes, with fish, was
wrecked on the Cobblers on the 3rd of March.
A. telegram from New York states that the
Arragon, steamer, from Bristol for that port
was stranded on Governor's Island, but would
probably come off. The Scotland, from Deme-
rara for New York, has been abandoned, water
logged; the crew were landed at St. John's by
the Jelin. The Ada, from Havannah for
Pensacola, ashore on the bar at the latter
place, has become a total wreak. The Venus,
from Darien, ashore at Doboy Bay, has become
a total wreck.

showing the several services for which a vote
"on account" is required for the year ending
March 31, 1873. The total is £1,772,850,
the estimate for the year having been

Yesterday afternoon Mr. Humphreys held
an inquest at the Green Man Tavern, Horton,
respecting the death of Charles Starkey, aged
28, who was murdered by Mr. Frederick
James, boot maker, carrying on business at
No. 103, Cumberland-street, Hackney-road.
Annie James, sister of the acoused, repeated

articles.title: "BAREFACED INJUSTICE."
articles.text:
"BAREFACED INJUSTICE."

The Daily News remarks that "ten days
ago a certain amount of consideration shown
to income-tax payers in the arrangements of
the budget seemed to warrant the hope thai
the severest Chancellor of the Exchequer of
recent times was relenting, and might in time
become, comparatively speaking, humane. But
it is to be feared that this was only a transient
illusion. Some facts respecting the working
of the budget changes which have transpired,
exhibit Mr. Lowe in his old hard and unre-
lenting mood. The principal dealers in.
coffee hold stocks on which the old
and higher duty has been paid, and
they have naturally expected that time
would be afforded them to sell out before the
newer duty came into operation, or else that
the difference between the new and old duties
should be repaid to them the latter being
perhaps the preferable alternative. It is
obviously unfair to take the merchant's money
for duty in advance, and then spring a mine
under him by reducing the duty, leaving him
with no means of reimbursing himself. Mr.
Lowe has beau appealed to, and all the reply
he vouchsafes in his letter is a bare non
possumus. 'Why the Chancellor should not do
what is evidently fair and right, he does not
vouchsafe to tell his correspondents, who will
be his helpless victims unless the House of
Commons Ahould very soon interpose for
their protection. Surely we are not brought
to such a pass that we are under the necessity
of augunienting the public revenue by bare-
faced injustice."

articles.text:
THE AMERICAN QUESTION.

A telegram from Philadelphia to the Times
says the United States Cabinet has postponed
the consideration of Earl Granville's Note
until to-morrow. The answer will be care-
fully (rained. According to otßoial intimation
the American position is unchanged. The
whole case must go to Geneva? .America leav-
ing all to the arbitrators' decision.
From Wabhington it is telegraphed through
Mr. Reuter, that the Evening Post says :
"The differenee of views between England
and America regarding the, indirect damages
involves no implication of bad faith on either
side. In the Washington Treaty Great 'Bri-
tain acted magnanimously, and made an
ample apology, which a great nation might
honourably accept as full redress for the in-
juries it had received. America agrees with
Great Britain that the indirect claims are in-
admissible, but they were advanced as an
argument for awarding a gross sum in the
shape of damages." The _Evening .Post regards
this form of settlement as feasible and desir-
able, and declares that the true policy of
America is the closest alliance and friendship
with Great Britain.

The Nolo York Tinaea is of opinion that the
United States Government cannot, withou
admitting carelessness, which should be fol
lowed by resignation, admit the indirect claim
to be either groundless or frivolous. Satisfac-
tion is expressed by the same paper at the
prospect of England submitting to the Geneva
arbitration.

In their annual report, issued yesterday,
the Church Estates Commissioners state that
during the past year they have transferred to
the Ecclesiastical Commissioners £30,000 in
respect of the surplus proceeds of enfranchise-
ments completed, the aggregate amount so
paid over being now £1,530,207, in addition
to £194,000 in respect of interest which has
accrued on the surplus. The transactions,
approved by the Commissioners between
August 1851 and March 1871, were 3,174 in
number' and the value in foe of the estates so
agreed to be dealt with amounted to about
£11,581,000. During the past year they
have approved the terms agreed upon in eight
oases of sales of reversions, the value in fee
of the estates so agreed to be dealt with being
approximately £9,000. The aggregate num-
ber of cases approved is therefore 3,182, and
the value of the property dealt with amounts
to about £11,500,000.

THE AGRICULTURAL LABOURERS.
To the Editor Of the BEE-HIVE.

Sin,--The crushed worm has turned at last,
to the horror of the farmers and landowners, to
.the great satisfaction of all men who sympa-
thise with the desolate and oppressed. If the
South Warwickshire labourers go on as they
have begun they appear certain to succeed.
What then? Oxfordshire, Worcester, and
Northampton will catch the protagion, and so
southward, eastward, westward, it will spread,
and result in a bitter and contracted struggle.
What the results of such a struggle may he it
is impossible to foretell. The extraneous aid
which so largely helps South Warwickshire will
not avail much when spread over half the
English counties, and the labourers, however
'staunch, will hardly be able to fight sucoess-
fully with their present Wretched pay. But
whether for good or evil, success in Warwick-
shire, will probably lead to a general move-
ment, a movement which must be regarded
seriously by the working classes of the towns..
Even at present, one of the chief weapons of
the agricultural labourers is migration; in the
future that weapon will be used much more ex-
tensively. We are told, and the statement is
not challenged, thiit one of the chief pauses of
the misery of the peasant is that the supply of
his labour is greater than the demand, and
that to succeed in his present attempt he must
make himself scarcer. Emigration :s difficult
and expensive, migration is easy and cheap.
But where shall the agricultural labourers
migrate? To the towns? Are not our towns
already overcrowded—so overcrowded that we
can scarcely bear the burden of pauperism?
'Surely we have unskilled labour enough and
-to spare in them already. If we add to our
present town population thousands of agricul-
tural immigrants, the rural labourer will only
be relieved at the expense of the town labourer.
Already the proportion Of town population to
rural population is too great—eleven millions.
to nine millions. There is nothing like it in
'Europe—even telgium, the most densely
populated country on the Continent,, has but
one-and-ciaalf millions in the towns, and five
-millions in the rural districts. Even now, we
suffer from the Continuous invasion of the cities
'by the rurals ; let Ili contemplate the possi-
bility of this invasion being doubled and
trebled in a few years' time. For the sake of
both the rural and town labourers such a mis-
fortune should be averted. The advanced
thinkers among the artizans have for a long
time held as an article of their politioal creed
that the waste landashould be cultivated. It
is time that doctrine should come to the front.
It can wait no longer, but presses for settle-
ment. By all means let the surplus agricul-
tural labour be drafted off, but not to the
'towns, where it would only thrust men out of
employment. With nine or ten millions of
.acres of waste laud capable of cultivation, our
Plain duty is to demand for the agricultural
labourers work in which they are already
killed, where they will displace no man,
where they will live in plenty, and. add to the
food-producing power of the country.

articles.text:
THE NOTTINGHAM FRAME-WORK
KNITTERS.

To the Editor of the BEE-HIVE.

SI am instructed by the workmen now
on strike in the Rib-Top Frame-work Knitters'
Association' of Nottingham, Hathern, and
Kirkby, to tender their united thanks to you
for giving such publicity to their cause in
your last week's issue, and earnestly implore
you to continue the same during the struggle.
The men are still out on strike, and as yet
have no prospect of going in, and again, there-
fore, we wish to impress upon the minds of
all trade unionists and trade societies our
great need of help, and earnestly invite
all to carefully investigate our case, and
stretch out to us the hand of unity and fellow-
ship, and render us what assistance may lie
in their power.
Last week our receipts were so small and
our numbers were so large that the committee
were only enabled to pay to the men 21. per
head; but I can assure you, sir, the men are
nothing daunted, even at this 'small sum, for
they feel that it is a gght of right against
?night, and are possessed with a firm deter-
mination to suffer anything rather than yield;
'and why? because it is a literal impossibility
for them to live at the present price of their
work. They might exist, but that is all;
they cannot live to the same privileges and
comforts of other artizans. 20s. per week and
the nine hours movement would be a boon
conferred upon these workmen they would
never forget; but they have been compelled
to work many more hours than that, for a deal
less money.
The employers know the workmen's position,
and no doubt are aware of the small amount
paid to ' them last Saturday, and perhaps
rejoice over this, and say amongst themselves,
" Ah, hunger is a sharp thorn; they will soon
have to bow to our dictu.m, and be compelled
to work at any price." But they little know
the minds of these men, and the courage which
lies in their hearts; they have been tampered
with a deal too much, until arbitration has
becoine entirely a mockery and a farce to
them. Therefore, being compelled to fight,
they are determined to win, or die in the
attempt.
Where, sir, are our groat hosiery manufac-
turers who are Members of Parliament, legis-
lators of the country, S. Morley' M.P., and
A. J. Mundella, M.P. ? will not they step
forward, and attempt to settle this great dis-
pute, and relieve the sufferings of over 200
families? as the workmen would be willing to
give in to anything which their superior juig-
ment should decide, if either one or both of
these gentlemen were made arbitrator between
them; and be it remembered these gentlemen
are numbered amongst our employers.
Hoping, sir, I have not trespassed too much
upon your space,—l remain, yours truly,
March 27, 1872. Ely. COOPER.

THE LONDON COACHMAKERS AND
• THE. NINE HOURS MOVEMENT, &a,
To the Editor of the BEE-II:Ivy.

Stu,—ln your issue of January 20tb, the
Committee of the Liverpool Operative Coaoh -
makers' Nino Hours' League addressed a com-
munication to the coaelinutkers of London
in whieh they regretted we were generally so
much behind hand in lessening the hours of
labour, &c., and attributed this state of things
to the fact that we were divided into a number
of "small clubs," and were hence powerless
to effect these changes; further intimating
that a general combination amongst ourselves,
or union with their own United Kingdom
Society, would secure the adoption of the
nine hours, and confer benefits otherwise un-
attainable.

I quite- expected, at the time the letter
appeared, it would have been replied to by
1501116 individual more prominently oonnected
with the London societies than I am myself;
but full two months having passed, and no
answer forthcoming, I am tempted to offer a
few remarks upon it myself. I think, Sir,
that courtesy to the writer, and our duty to
the public, demand an answer. It was ad-
dressed to us for the purpose of forwarding
what the authors believed to be a good cause;
that they did so believe their readiness to
submit their ideas to publie criticism is a
sufficient proof, if proof were required. While
giving Mr. M'Nay (the writer) and the com-
mittee credit for the very best intentions, we
trust, in presenting a different view of the
question, they will equally believe us to be
sincere. We say then that we are publicly
appealed to to assist in forwarding what is
believed would be a public benefit; and what-
ever our opinion may be, we ought to express
it. The questions involved affect the com-
munity. either for good. or for harm, and to
treat it with indifference would be to shirk a
public duty. The undertaking is not alto-
gether free from difficulty, from the fact
already mentioned that we are divided into a.
number (ten) or small societies amounting to
upwards of a thousand members, and there
are fully at 3 many non-members. The latter
include, amongst their number, many liberty-
loving individuals, who have fled from the
restraints of country life, and in many in-
stances from the restraints imposed by
the T.TrOted Kingdom Booiety, to the

great city and centre of freedom, and to
bring these men to observe rules, other
than those imposed by nature and the law of
the land, would not be found all easy matter;
nor would the diffieulty be less with great
numbers of the society men. Besides this
diversity of opinion, and the determination to
act upon it, there is in London perpetual
change going on. For instance, at present
a man might be a society man, but before this
letter is in print—if printed at all—he might
be a non-society man or an employer. Trans-
formations of this kind are continually occur-
ring, and again and again repeated by the same
individual. So that a society man on pro-
claiming his opinions might be called upon to
continue the discussion as a non-society man,
and a journeyman under the necessity of de-
fending his argument when in the position of
an employer. A man, therefore, can only say
—like Mr. M'Nay—what he believes to be
right to all parties, the public included.
While, therefore, everything must bo sub-
servient to the broad principle of right, yet
many years a member of one of these clubs, I
am entitled to be heard in the capacity of a
society man. A necessity exists that I should
be so heard, from the fact that since the publica-
tion of the letter in question, a movement has
been made for the purpose of inviting the
club, of which I am a member, to that of the
U.K.S., and we wish to point out a few things
that at present stand in the way of such. a
consumation. I must inform you, sir, that
coachmaking differs greatly from many other
employments, In trades, where grearnumbers
of men in close contact with, and much
depending the one upon the other, are engaged
about large undertakings where there is no
chance of men with small means becoming
employers? some' sort of colleetive under-
standing is a necessity; but a coachmaker
may be said to work alone, and on objecting
to the position of journeyman can, with
little else than a good name, start
on his own account, and, as already said, there
are plenty that do so. We say, therefore,
that collective interference in our case with
employers is altogether wrong, and abstain
from it accordingly. But with the tr.K.S. it
is otherwise, and we admit that, spread wide
as they are, they have far greater excuse for
it than we have. .1 believe I am right in stating
that when a misunderstanding occurs between a
member of the U.K.S. and his employer about
price, time, apprentices, or non-society men,
the society steps between the two, and, if
possible, settles it for them; but a London
coachmakor would hardly more think of intro-
ducing a society, or any third party, between
hiinself and his employer, for purposes of coer-
cion, than he would think of doing the same
thing in his domestic affairs. With him an
engagement is something that concerns only
those who are parties to it, whether the engage-
moot be with a large employeror with a member
of the U.K.S., and either party inviting or
permitting the interference of a third com-
mits a breach of faith, that is necessarily fol-
lowed by distrust and the absence of good and
right feeling. Sometimes the U.K.S. fails to
settle a grievance, and then it comes to what
may be termed lighting. Not a man to man
fight, but it is the society, or a large number,
against one man. But a London coachmaker
prefers to fight his own battle. If he sought
the aid of a society against his employer he
would be regarded in the light of a man who,
on being challenged to a single combat,
stead Of declining the offer, or training him-
self for the business, procured a number of
others to help him vanquish his opponent. Such
a fellow, and those who aided him, would c er-
tainly be looked upon as cowards, while he who
fought alone against the odds would win the
admiration and support of everyone. This,
we say, is a parallel of what would occur
were we to bring a combination to bear upon
an employer. It is said the masters combine
against the men, but we say that an unneces-
sary combination, whether for the purpose of
raising profits or for raising wages, is a
wrong, and hence a weakness, and, no man
has anything to fear from that source, even if
true. If, says the London coachmaker, there
is to be combination, and odds on one side,
the combination and odds must be against
him. If fight he must, he will, in any case,
have the honour and advantage of fighting
alone, He will have no help, because it only
encouraged him in bowardice, relieves him
from the necessity of training himself for
the battle of life; a battle in which, in
reality, no one can either help or hinder him.
Until this manly doctrine is acknowledged
and practised by the 1.T.K.5., amalgamation
would be a misfortune to all concerned.

Again, as regards the Nino Hours, the po-
sition of London coub makers differs from
most other trades. For instance, less than
twenty years ago we used to work twelve
hours to the day. It has been reduced to
eleven for tho reason that it was a waste, or
an abuse, of time to be in the shop so long.
The same thing has been said of eleven hours.
it has been urged that in ten hours a man, as
a rule, will do as much work`as he can do at
all; and, in some instances, the ten hours has
been adopted. But no one would think of
using those arguments in favour of nine
hours; all admit there would be a less

manner, and by a similar and an explainable
process, were coachmakers to obtain money by
combination, the poorest people want, and
have to suffer for it, though it must be men'
tioned that nature at once sets to work, br a
well known process, to rectify this bybringiog
the evil down upon the heads of those who
offend her laws. Instead of ooachtnakers
combining to enforce individual selfishness
and individual self-will, inflicting immediate
injury upon the poorest, and quickly bringing
this same injury upon themselves—l say,
instead of doing this, Nature or the Christian
religion would have them exert themselves to
raise the condition of the poorest—a thing

It is said by the men of the U.K.S. that
the employers are combining, and therefore
it is necessary the workmen should be
"strongly united." I would like to mention

articles.title: BRIGHTON REVIEW.
articles.text:
THE BRIGHTON REVIEW.

The great proportion of the volunteers who
intended to take phrt in the review last Mon-
day had gone down previously, and the wet
weather in London at early morning had but
a very slight effect upon the general strength
of the corps in the field. The railway arrange-
ments provided for the transport of 23,488
men, of whom 5,324 were to travel from Lon-
don Bridge to Brighton, 5,848 from London
Bridge to Lewes 3,089 from Victoria to Lewes,
2,343 from Victoria to Brighton, and 530
from Kensington to Brighton; but probably
not more than half of the number remained
for Monday morning's trains, which conse-
quently left with many carriages entirely
unoccupied. The traffic from London Bridge
and Victoria on Monday differed somewhat
from that of former years, and was a severe
test of the company's organisation, owing to
the fact of its being necessary that the two
points of departure, for Lewes and for Brighton,
should be kept distinct. Under the manage-
ment of the station-master, the staff proved
quite equal to the occasion, and the arrange-
ments were carried out in a most satisfactory
manner. From London Bridge to Lewes and
Brighton the trains were timed to run simul-
taneously at 5.0 a.m., 5.20, 5.35, and 5.50;
but these times were not strictly adhered to,
apparently from the fact of some of the corps
not arriving to time.
There was no danger that the crowd would
at the outset interfere with the movements of
the troops, for the walk from the town to the
racecourse had already satisfied most pedes-
trians, and the attacking forces were at least
two miles ahead, and could only be recognised
by the dense appearance which they presented
in the valley or against the crest of a hill ;
and by the occasional sputtering of the
skirmishers in front. Presently, however,
there was a cry of "They come !1' and a cer-
tain activity was discernible amongst the re-
serves. The hills that touched the horizon
now became lined with a long file, of skir-
mishers, and the fight haying begun in real
earnest, was watched with ignorant, but none
the less unbroken attention. Presently, too,
the batteries began to play in evory direction,
and vast clouds of smoke swept over the hills.
Then the heavy 18-pounder battery was
brought up from the reserve and posted near
the south side of Warren Farm. The opera-
tions of the artillery became immediately the
centre of attraction • and notwithstanding the
deafening effect which their reports had upon
the ears of the bystanders, they persisted in
pressing round each one, with both ears
securely protected, and ready with a chorus of
exclamations when the word "Fire I" was
given. How the fight went, who was winning
or losing, nobody seemed to know or care
about, and even when the extreme left wing
opened a murderous fire upon some person or
persons unknown, the strategical meaning of
the manceuvre was not in the least inquired
into. There was a sudden halt after this, and
a general feeling that it was All over,"
whereupon a "skedaddle" to the Grand Stand
became a matter of primitive necessity. The
crowd had now become immense, and the
crush just about the Stand was at one moment
inconvenient; but when it became plain that
there was as good a view to be obtained any-
where else the crowd spread itself with in-
telligent rapidity on both sides, leaving the
course open for the troops, who could be seen
massed in dense squares about half a mile to
the north.

,
Immediately on the conclusion of the sham
fight the various regiments were marched,
some independently and some in brigades, to
the racecourse, where the march took place in
the reverse direction to that of previous years,
The saluting point was dose to the corner of
the Brighton end of the Grand Stand, and the
salutes wtre taken by Major-General Ellice,
as Commanding-in-Chief. The Artillery did
not march past, it being found impossible to
get the guns into position in time. The first
to pass the general was the handful of the
Ist Sussex Light Horse. Lord Ranelagh's
brigade headed the infantry, and it was
noticed that among the Sussex corps there was
a great deal of changing step when near the
saluting point. The Ist A. B. Sussex were in
particular desperately out of step, the dressing
was bad, and there was more talking in the
ranks than ought to have been. The South
Middlesex Rifles marched past in a highly

creditable manner, its also did. the Artists, the
Lancashire corps several of the Surrey corps,
and. the let Middlesex Engineers. After the first
contingent had passed came the detachment of
the 19th Hussars, who seem the ideal of
dashing little horsemen; and then the crowd
broke in, thinking all was over. At the order
of "fours about" the Hussars reversed their
front, iind cleared the course with great
dexterity, remaining on it to keep it when
cleared. Of the regiments at whose head
General Lysons marched past those most
noticed were the 2nd Tower Hamlets, the Ist
Hon. Artillery Company's infantry, the
London Rifle Brigade, the Victorias, the St.
Georges, the 37th Middlesex, the London
Scottish, and the London Irish. But the
marching, as a whole, was far from satisfactory.
After the march the troops went straight down
to the parade, with scarcely a stoppage, and
again assembled on the Level, whence by
detachments they were conducted to the. rail-
way-station, and shipped for London.
